- list 1 of 3‘To challenge deadly blockade’: New flotilla mission sets sail for Gaza
- list 2 of 3US imposes sanctions on Turkish bank, prompting legal threat
- list 3 of 3At least five killed in Sudan’s South Kordofan in attack by rebel group
The polygraph examinations took place last month after news outlets published several reports highlighting severe drops in key weapons supplies, including long-range missiles and Patriot air defence interceptors. US officials had pushed back on these reports, insisting their weapons stockpiles were more than sufficient.
In a statement to the NYT, Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell declined to address internal administrative or investigative actions directly, but emphasised that the department takes leaks of national security information “extremely seriously and investigates accordingly”.
“Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world,” Parnell added.
The Joint Staff, which consists of between 1,500 and 2,000 military and civilian staff, plays a key role in coordinating operational strategy, policy and war planning with combat commands globally.
Unprecedented move
Sources familiar with the inquiry told the NYT that the aggressive push was designed not only to identify the individuals behind the disclosures, but also to deter potential future leakers.
Legal and military experts say the scale of the investigation is unprecedented, as the top ranks of the US armed forces have never undergone widespread polygraph testing in modern history.
The move follows widespread reporting on how active military operations involving Iran have severely strained US weapon reserves, causing internal debates over the broader direction of the conflict.
US President Donald Trump has repeatedly pushed officials to crack down on unauthorised disclosures. In addition to calling for strict enforcement, Trump has publicly branded critical media coverage regarding munition shortages and the administration’s handling of the conflict in Iran as “treasonous”.
The persistent leaks have deepened an atmosphere of deep distrust inside the Pentagon, which current and former officials attribute to the management style of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
Operating alongside a tight circle of close aides, Hegseth has ousted or blocked the promotions of at least 80 generals, admirals and senior officials during his tenure, the report said.
The Pentagon has launched multiple leak probes in response to media coverage of Hegseth’s leadership, even as he faced criticism for sharing sensitive operational details in a Signal group chat.
The internal tensions escalated further last month when the Defence Department fired the top editor and publisher of Stars and Stripes, an independent, government-funded military news publication.
Staff members said the move was direct retaliation for stories detailing deteriorating conditions on board the aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln.
Despite the mounting friction, Trump has backed Hegseth, publicly praising his performance as “fantastic”.

articles.title: UK sends aircraft carrier to strengthen NATO defenses
articles.body:
- HMS Queen Elizabeth departs Portsmouth on September 5 for a three-month deployment, serving as NATO's afloat command platform for the Allied Reaction Force.
- The Royal Navy took command of the alliance's high-readiness maritime force from Spain in July, and Queen Elizabeth will return to UK high-readiness carrier duty from HMS Prince of Wales in 2027.
HMS Queen Elizabeth is due to leave Portsmouth Naval Base at 6:20 p.m. on Saturday, September 5, carrying more than 800 sailors on a three-month deployment around British and northern European waters, according to UK Defence Journal.
The deployment is the first extended sea period for the 65,000-tonne carrier since it took on a new NATO role in July: serving as the alliance’s afloat command platform for the Allied Reaction Force (Maritime), NATO’s high-readiness naval crisis-response formation. It’s the first time either of the UK’s two Queen Elizabeth-class carriers has held that specific command role. The UK Royal Navy assumed leadership of the force on July 1, taking over from the Spanish Navy, with Rear Admiral Mark Anderson and his Portsmouth-based staff now running it for a 12-month rotation. If activated, the force is designed to assemble warships, naval aircraft and support vessels within ten days to respond to a crisis anywhere in NATO’s area of responsibility.
Over the coming three months, Queen Elizabeth will train alongside allied forces to build up the crew’s ability to run high-end naval operations and command a multinational force under pressure, according to the Royal Navy. The ship will also work through advanced training under the Royal Navy’s Fleet Operational Standards and Training organization, covering the full spectrum of modern naval warfare.
“We’ve returned from summer leave rested and ready for the next phase of our training,” said Captain Claire Thompson, commanding officer of HMS Queen Elizabeth. “Sailing this autumn is a key milestone for both our NATO commitment, as the Afloat Command Platform and also on our journey back to the Royal Navy’s ‘very high readiness’ aircraft carrier, a duty we will resume from our sister ship HMS Prince of Wales in 2027. Sailing with an embarked battle staff, integration and training is essential whilst relearning the skills required to conduct safe and effective aviation as we ensure that we are prepared to deliver operational activity at the heart of NATO should it be required.”
The autumn deployment is doing double duty. Alongside its NATO command responsibilities, Queen Elizabeth is working through the training cycle that will eventually return it to the role of UK principal carrier at very high readiness, a status HMS Prince of Wales currently holds. That handover, along with participation in major NATO exercises, is scheduled to continue through 2027, when Queen Elizabeth is due to take over from Prince of Wales as the UK’s flagship and high-readiness strike carrier.
This is not the first time a Queen Elizabeth-class carrier has worn a NATO hat. Prince of Wales served as NATO’s afloat command platform for the alliance’s rapid response force in 2022, and Queen Elizabeth itself briefly came under NATO operational control during the Neptune Strike exercise in 2023. What’s changed since is the underlying force structure: NATO replaced its old Response Force with the current three-tiered model, including the Allied Reaction Force, following the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine and the alliance’s 2023 Vilnius summit, and this deployment marks the first time either British carrier has held the maritime command role under that newer structure.
The Royal Navy said the deployment sits within a broader pattern of British contributions to NATO deterrence. More than 1,000 UK personnel currently serve in NATO command posts, and Britain leads the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps from its headquarters in Gloucestershire. Separately, the UK maintains an 800-strong battlegroup in Estonia, has RAF Typhoon fighters defending NATO airspace over Romania, and operates P-8 Poseidon and RC-135W Rivet Joint surveillance aircraft around the Baltic Sea.
Britain also assigns its nuclear deterrent to NATO’s defense and, under its Defence Investment Plan, intends to join the alliance’s Dual Capable Aircraft nuclear mission using F-35A fighters, a step that would put the UK in the group of NATO members that can carry nuclear weapons on aircraft rather than only via its submarine-based deterrent.

articles.title: Air Force Speeding Up New Low-Cost Drone Program after Heavy MQ-9 Losses Against Iran
articles.body:
The Air Force is accelerating its plans to field an MQ-9A replacement in the wake of heavy Reaper losses in operations against Iran, top officials said Sept. 3, and they’re targeting a price point of just $10 million per aircraft.
Back in July, the Air Force and the Defense Innovation Unit announced plans to develop a low-cost drone to do all the missions that an MQ-9 can do today, and when necessary fly in groups to overwhelm an enemy’s anti-drone capabilities and force them to expend large numbers of munitions. They called the effort Massed Modular Aircraft, or MMA.
At the time, officials said they wanted to have a prototype to test fly within 21 months of a contract, and then 20 mission-ready aircraft by fiscal 2031 to achieve initial operating capability.
Now, though, officials are targeting a more ambitious timeline. During a media roundtable at the Pentagon, DIU military deputy Maj. Gen. Joseph Kunkel said the MMA program will try to follow DIU’s typical timeframe of prototyping a system within a year of a contract, and then fielding it at scale within three years—as soon as 2029.
Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s new chief modernization officer, said those goals changed “fairly recently,” when Air Force Secretary Troy Meink “called us in and said ‘You need to move faster.’”
That urgency, Niemi acknowledged, came at least partly in response to the significant losses the MQ-9 fleet has taken in the past year or so during operations against Iran and Iranian-backed militias. Since the start of the Iran war, the Air Force has lost at least 45 MQ-9s, roughly a quarter of its fleet. The service was already thinking about what it needed to succeed the MQ-9 as a medium-altitude intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance platform, but Niemi said the combat losses pushed it to move faster.
“Although we have plenty of MQ-9As today, we are going through them at a rate that is concerning to us,” Niemi said.
Replacing, Not Reinventing, the MQ-9
The MQ-9 has long been a workhorse of the Air Force fleet, valued by combatant commanders for its long endurance, loitering ability, and ability to combine strike and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance capabilities. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach called the Reaper the “most valuable player” of Operation Epic Fury in a May congressional hearing.
Unsurprisingly, then, officials said they were eager to replace the ones lost in combat. Niemi said the Air Force has “spent a lot of time and energy” in recent months trying to figure out how to do so and found “there’s not a lot of good options to immediately replace those aircraft.”
The Air Force considered General Atomics’ MQ-9B, a larger and more complex—and more expensive—version of the MQ-9A, Niemi said. Ultimately, officials concluded the MQ-9B was not the right choice because the Air Force needed something more “attritable,” or inexpensive enough to be fielded in large numbers and easily replaced if lost in combat.
“If you don’t like losing an MQ-9A that cost on the order of $50 million, with the sensors, you’re probably not going to like losing an MQ-9B at a higher price point,” Niemi said.
For that reason, the Air Force decided to go all-in on the MMA concept. The Air Force plans to field at least 180 of the drones, Niemi said, but probably more than that.
In order to move fast and keep costs down, Niemi said the Air Force plans to “accept prudent risk” on the MMA program. Kunkel also said the Air Force wants “significantly increased levels of competition” to keep costs down.
As the Air Force wrote out what attributes MMA drones would need, Niemi added, it tried to allow as much flexibility as possible and not include hyper-specific requirements that “push technology to the very edge.”
“When that happens, you’re going to pay a lot for it, because it’s hard to do,” Niemi said. “It takes a lot of engineering, cutting-edge science, emergent technologies, things like that. So we’re trying to be more aligned with sort of an ‘80 percent is good enough,’ [using] mature technologies” approach.
That means MMA won’t have the latest and greatest flight control systems, engines, or manufacturing processes, he said—and they’ll actually resemble the MQ-9 in some key ways: they’ll likely have long-aspect wings and will likely be powered by turboprop engines.
One way officials are looking to differ from the MQ-9, though, are higher levels of autonomy and automation than the MQ-9A has today, Niemi said—“more mouse clicks and keyboard strokes instead of a stick and throttle.” That will reduce the number of Airmen needed to operate MMA drones and allow a single Airman to operate multiple drones simultaneously.
At the same time, Niemi said MMAs won’t have the same level of autonomy as the Air Force’s flagship autonomous drone program, Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
“It’s not going out and autonomously finding targets and employing weapons,” Niemi said of the MMA drone. “It’s more like a truck that’s carrying packages, whether it’s a sensor package or whether it’s a weapon, to a point where it can be employed.”
CCAs and MMAs
While CCAs and MMAs will both be unmanned and have some kind of autonomy software, Niemi was quick to note there will be major differences between the two.
“They’re going to look very different,” Niemi said. The MMA is “going to look like an MQ-9, and [CCA is] going to look more like a fighter, like you’ve seen in the current too CCAs that we’re flying.”
The Air Force wants MMA drones to be able to fly about 4,000 miles—more than twice the expected range of autonomous Collaborative Combat Aircraft drones—and carry a heavy payload, although they will be slower than CCAs, Niemi said.
Those differences extend to price, too—while the Air Force is targeting $10 million for an MMA drone, it’s hoping for $20 million per CCA once they reach full production. Those costs are for just the base aircraft, excluding sensors, weapons or other equipment that might be loaded onto them.
From an acquisition perspective, the Air Force is hoping to use the same methods across the CCA and MMA programs to keep costs down and production simple.
That includes moving quickly to award contracts and keeping several vendors on contract to provide a variety of drones. Like CCAs, MMA drones will also use open architecture, Niemi said. That will ensure the drones have standardized interfaces and could be easily upgraded with newer sensor packages or weapons capabilities, even from different vendors, he said. This would also allow MMAs to be tailored with the gear needed for a particular mission.
“If you want to build a package that’s going to go on this new aircraft, as long as it conforms to this [standardized interface], we can do it very speedily and very readily,” Niemi said. “That’s something we struggle with at the opposite end of the spectrum, something like the F-35, where it’s very very hard to incorporate new things onto it, because of the construct and the architecture of that system.”
The Air Force also wants manufacturers to be able to produce MMA drones in large numbers, Niemi said, but also be able to ramp production up or down as needed, such as if the Air Force started losing large numbers in a heated conflict. Keeping MMAs simple is the best way to ensure that production flexibility, he said.
“If you wanted to suddenly ramp up production of something like an F-35, it’s not a limiting factor so much as money, as the ability to build out your production capacity and actually crank more of those things out,” Niemi said. “And the more complex the aircraft, the harder that problem is. … In major combat operations, depending on who you’re fighting, we could be losing dozens [of MMA drones] a day, and so you have to figure out how do you adjust the industrial capacity in order to make [necessary production levels] happen.”
General Atomics, which also makes the MQ-9, is planning to pitch a newly designed drone it calls Wildfire for the MMA program.
“Our new Wildfire aircraft addresses all of the concerns posed by the MMA solicitation,” General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in a statement to reporters. “We can deliver years earlier and maintain the same high quality. You can have everything that makes Reaper special, plus more, at a price that doesn’t break the bank.”

articles.title: Combat Continues as Russia Rejects Ceasefire
articles.body:
The Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) announced on Saturday, Sept. 5, that combat operations are ongoing following Russia’s refusal to agree to a proposed mutual ceasefire between Sept. 5 and Sept. 9.
The General Staff of the AFU told Ukrainska Pravda and Suspilne that a unilateral ceasefire is impossible because it would endanger military personnel, adding that defensive tasks are being executed in full according to plan.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Dmytro Filatov, commander of the 1st Separate Assault Regiment, stated that while the General Staff issued orders restricting strikes at an operational depth, no limitations were imposed on tactical-level combat.
The Russian Ministry of Defense confirmed its refusal to observe a temporary truce, publishing a report on Saturday detailing its overnight combined strikes on industrial facilities in the Dnipropetrovsk region and logistics and energy infrastructure in the Mykolaiv and Odesa regions.
Overnight strikes and proposed diplomatic pause
The Russian Defense Ministry’s claims correspond with reported strikes across southern and central Ukraine early Saturday.
A Russian ballistic missile struck an industrial enterprise in Kamianske in the Dnipropetrovsk region, killing four people and injuring five others. Regional authorities reported that three individuals were hospitalized, including a 30-year-old woman requiring intensive care.
In Mykolaiv, consecutive jet-powered “Shahed” drone strikes hit an Epicenter shopping center late Friday and early Saturday, injuring a 72-year-old man and a 17-year-old girl and triggering a large fire.
The Skeleton Putin Needs
The Saturday attacks follow a Friday strike that damaged a nine-story residential building in Boryspil, Kyiv region, where a fire broke out on the roof and in an upper-floor apartment.
The sustained aerial campaign comes despite Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s Friday announcement proposing a mutual halt to airstrikes.
The proposal was intended to accommodate the upcoming diplomatic mission of US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who are scheduled to visit Moscow and Kyiv this weekend.

articles.title: U.S. Investigates Deadly Strike on Wedding in Iran, Vance Says
articles.body:
The U.S. is investigating a strike on a wedding in southern Iran, Vice President J.D. Vance said Thursday, as reports suggest American weapons killed at least five people and injured dozens of others.
“We’re investigating it because obviously we care,” Vance told reporters. “We want to know.”
The strike represents the U.S.’s latest controversial action in its war with Iran, raising questions about its conduct and civilian harm. Washington and Tehran have escalated their attacks this week, ending a lull in hostilities since July.
But Vance said he was “extremely skeptical” about reports coming from Iranian state media, arguing they have “not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far.”
Iranian state media reported that a residential building in Kuhestak was attacked on Tuesday evening, where a wedding was being celebrated. Among the casualties was a 4-year-old kid. Reuters and the New York Times independently verified footage from the scene and found that a wedding was taking place when the building was struck.
Iran's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that it “will respond to these savage crimes with firmness”—and responded to a broader barrage of American attacks by launching missiles and drones at sites used by the U.S. in Middle East states. The Iranian Red Crescent Society, a humanitarian group, also urged a probe from the International Criminal Court to assess potential violations of international law.
The U.S. Central Command said Wednesday it was already looking into reports of the incident but argued that the “U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps],” referring to Iran’s armed forces branch.
Vance also defended U.S. military action, telling reporters: “If we do make mistakes, again, this is a big difference between us and Iran: when our military makes mistakes, they learn from them to try to get better from them.”
What we know about the strike
On the evening of Sept. 1, CENTCOM reported strikes on military targets, including “air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites.”
Iranian media later reported four deaths and at least 68 injured in Kuhestak, a coastal town on the Strait of Hormuz, where trade has been bottlenecked since the start of the U.S.-Iran war in late February. The strikes happened at around 9:30 p.m. local time, per the Red Crescent.
Analyses of footage from the incident conducted by Reuters and the New York Times reveal that wedding guests were gathered in a Kuhestak building. Amid the celebration, what was likely a U.S. munition hit the building and, as the Times put it, “brought down the roof.”
Experts told Reuters and the Times that weapon fragments seen in Iranian media were consistent with what Americans have used.
The attacks on Kuhestak also hit a communications tower roughly 100 m away from the building. A human rights group told the Associated Press that one of the four people initially reported killed—a 16-year-old—was struck by shrapnel near the tower rather than at the wedding. Iranian state television said Thursday that a 22-year-old woman had since died in hospital following the strike, bringing the reported death toll to five.
Axios reported that CENTCOM Commander Adm. Brad Cooper ordered an internal review of the strike.
Civilian casualties raise concern
The Red Crescent sent a letter to the International Criminal Court Wednesday calling for “an independent, impartial, thorough, and effective investigation,” citing the “civilian character” of the strike’s location.
The organization also argued that under the Rome Statute, intentionally directing attacks on civilians and knowingly launching a clearly excessive attack may constitute “war crimes.” However, both Iran and the U.S. are nonparties to the Rome Statute, so the ICC does not have automatic jurisdiction over them.
Still, “the laws of war state that civilians are protected from military attacks,” Melanie O’Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia, tells TIME. “A wedding is not a military objective, particularly in a civilian residential building. It is clear that there was a direct missile hit to the home. This would render the attack unlawful.”
It’s also not the U.S.’s first involvement in strikes that hit civilian structures without obvious military use and that endangered or killed civilians. On the first day of the war with Iran on Feb. 28, a U.S. Tomahawk missile hit a primary school in Minab—just 30 km (18 mi) away from Kuhestak—where more than 100 children were killed.
O’Brien, however, says she is skeptical about any result from the U.S.-led investigation of the wedding strike: “The U.S. track record is to only investigate when allegations gain significant public traction, and even when any convictions occur, the penalties are minor or pardons are given.”

articles.title: Why is Trump threatening to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain again, now?
articles.body:
Why is Trump threatening to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain again, now?
As oil tanker struck off Kharg island, Trump threatens one of the remaining parts of Iran’s nuclear complex.
United States President Donald Trump says Washington may strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain “very soon”, in just the latest in a series of threats he has made against the heavily fortified underground site located next to the bombed-out Natanz enrichment complex.
Just hours after he made that threat, an Iranian oil tanker off Kharg Island was struck by four US missiles, according to Iranian news outlet Khabar Fouri. Kharg Island is the main hub for Iran’s oil exports, handling about 90 percent.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iran war: Why US midterms could be a pivotal moment
- list 2 of 4South Korea mulls ‘contributions’ in Strait of Hormuz
- list 3 of 4Diesel price hits all-time high in US amid Iran war woes
- list 4 of 4US imposes sanctions on Turkish bank, prompting legal threat
Trump made the threat against Pickaxe Mountain as he was speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, saying the US knows “everybody that’s moving at Pickaxe” and across Iran.
His remarks echoed a similar threat he made back in mid-July, when he stated on the Hugh Hewitt Show: “We’re going to take out Pickaxe Mountain. Tell the Iranians to be ready … We’ll probably give Pickaxe a shot relatively soon.”
The latest threat comes more than six months into the war that the US and Israel launched on Iran on February 28, amid mixed messages about the war from the Trump administration.
On Friday, Trump sought to downplay the war in Iran, calling it “small potatoes”, while a day earlier, at a White House news briefing, Vice President JD Vance appeared to suggest the conflict had cooled and to shrug off an alleged US strike on a wedding in southern Iran with “sometimes things happen“.
At a White House briefing this week, Vance said of the conflict with Iran that he “wouldn’t call it a war” and claimed there was “no active shooting right now”.
But the US and Iran have exchanged attacks this week, including a US hit close to Iran’s oil infrastructure on Kharg Island.
Meanwhile, talks related to Iran’s nuclear programme have remained in limbo since a 60-day negotiating window expired in mid-August without a deal.
Iran says it is not undertaking any work at the Natanz nuclear site.
Its Khatam al-Anbiya central military headquarters has warned that bombing the nearby mountain would amount to a renewal of war across the region, at a time when the Trump administration would prefer to keep the war contained before pivotal mid-term elections.
So why has Pickaxe Mountain become the latest focus of Trump’s threats – again?
What is Pickaxe Mountain?
Known in Iran as Kuh-e Kolang Gaz La, the site sits roughly 220km (140 miles) south of the capital Tehran, in Isfahan province, and just 2km (1.2 miles) from the Natanz enrichment plant.
US intelligence reports indicate that the facility has been excavated deep inside the mountain, beneath hundreds of metres of solid granite rock, to protect it from powerful bombs designed to penetrate bunkers.
The main chambers are thought to lie at least 100 metres (330ft) underground.
Some Western analysts have speculated that the mountain was intended to house an undeclared enrichment plant, a hedge against attacks on Iran’s known facilities.
The Institute for Science and International Security, which tracks the site by satellite, has assessed that it is still under construction and not yet operational.
However, Iran has always maintained that it is developing a nuclear power programme only, and does not have plans to build a nuclear weapon.
Why does Pickaxe Mountain matter?
Because it is intact.
Pickaxe Mountain was left alone during the US’s June 2025 strikes on Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan at the end of the 12-day Israel war on Iran, and has escaped the current war almost entirely; the Institute for Science and International Security has recorded only the destruction of a vehicle on a nearby spoil pile.
With Iran’s centrifuge manufacturing base and enrichment halls at other sites damaged in the war, analysts see the tunnels as the most obvious place for Tehran to rebuild: For component production, assembly or enrichment of uranium.
The Wall Street Journal reported in July that Israel had passed Washington intelligence suggesting thousands of centrifuges had been moved inside the facility late last year, a claim the US has not confirmed.
Trump has been less alarmist than Israel.
Centrifuges only matter if there is uranium to put through them; the machines concentrate uranium gas, and without a supply of it they cannot produce anything.
How much damage has been done to Iran’s nuclear sites?
According to most estimates, a considerable amount.
The European Council on Foreign Relations estimates that the 2025 strikes likely destroyed many of the roughly 18,000 centrifuges then operating at Iran’s Natanz and Fordow facilities, along with several centrifuge production sites and Ardakan, Iran’s only yellowcake milling plant. Yellowcake is powdered uranium concentrate obtained from milled uranium ore.
Nearly 4,000 additional centrifuges were installed but idle at the time; however, they may have survived the strikes.
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) confirmed further damage to the entrance buildings of Natanz’s underground enrichment plant in March 2026, although it detected no additional impact on the plant itself.
The Institute for Science and International Security reported in June that tunnel entrances at all three main sites remain sealed, that there is no evidence of any enrichment taking place, and that the centrifuge programme still appears to have been destroyed.
Didn’t Trump say Iran’s nuclear sites had already been destroyed?
Yes. After the June 2025 attacks, Trump said the three sites had been “completely and totally obliterated”.
However, just days later, a leaked preliminary US Defence Intelligence Agency assessment concluded that the sites had been significantly damaged but not destroyed, estimating that the strikes had set Iran’s nuclear programme back by less than six months.
The situation today remains unclear.
Iran is currently believed to be holding about 440kg (970lb) of uranium enriched to 60 percent. A 90-percent threshold of enriched uranium is needed to produce a nuclear weapon.
No inspector has entered the bombed sites, and Trump’s framing has shifted from “obliteration” to a promise to hit any site where Iran is “even thinking about nuclear”.
What do we know about Iran’s nuclear programme?
Less than at any point in two decades.
Just before the US-Israel attacks on Iran in June 2025, the IAEA verified about 10 tonnes of enriched uranium in total, including the 440kg stockpile enriched to 60 percent.
In theory, this amount of enriched uranium – should it be enriched to 90 percent – is enough to produce more than 10 nuclear warheads, IAEA chief Rafael Grossi told Al Jazeera in early March. It is unclear where this stock may be, however.
Iran suspended cooperation with the agency after the strikes, and the IAEA now says it has no way to report on the size, location or composition of that stockpile, though it believes much of the 60-percent material is bottled up in tunnels at Isfahan.
On Friday, Trump claimed again that the US had prevented Iran from developing a nuclear weapon, arguing that Washington’s intervention had protected Israel and the wider Middle East.
Tehran insists the programme is peaceful, and has dismissed Washington’s focus on Pickaxe Mountain as a manufactured pretext for attacking it.

articles.title: ‘Guilt by association’: why seven international aid workers were killed in Israeli airstrike
articles.body:
Seven aid workers killed in an airstrike in Gaza were marked as targets under an Israeli military practice of establishing guilt by association, a Guardian investigation shows.
A top Israeli military prosecutor announced last month that he would not pursue criminal proceedings for the April 2024 incident in which drones fired missiles at three clearly marked World Central Kitchen (WCK) cars soon after they had escorted a food aid delivery to Gaza. Three British humanitarian workers along with an Australian, a Palestinian, a Pole and a dual US-Canadian national were killed.
The official Israel Defense Forces (IDF) version of events pointed to specific mistakes made by a handful of officers. The victims of the strike were also blamed for hiring armed guards to protect a food aid convoy and for allegedly “deviating” from their agreed route.
However, interviews with senior Israeli officers involved in the incident or familiar with the official Israel investigation suggest it glossed over the role played in the killings by a common IDF practice used to designate targets, which endangers aid workers and civilians in general, especially when combined with the army’s open-ended mission to end Hamas’s civil control in Gaza.
More than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed by the Israeli military in the three years of the Gaza war. The army’s own internal data suggests more than three-quarters of the dead have been civilians.
The reserve colonel who ordered the strikes, Nochi Mendel, said the WCK workers became potential targets after they had a brief encounter, lasting just minutes, with armed guards assumed to be from Hamas (an assumption later shown to be groundless).
He deemed them to have “mixed together” with alleged Hamas militants, where mixing together was defined as being “near them, talking, playing, hanging out and so on”. Asked whether the presence of armed men made the entire convoy a target, Mendel replied: “Certainly.”
He concluded: “They were not innocent because they were connected to Hamas.”
Mendel was referring to a general policy of haflala, “incrimination”, which gives commanders in the field wide discretion on designating someone as a “terrorist”, including those “incriminated” by association. The manner in which haflala is to be applied in a given sector is often conveyed in a commander’s mission brief delivered verbally to other officers.
He said his unit had been commended by the army hierarchy for its involvement in several strikes on what were deemed to be Hamas attempted commandeering of aid. “They applauded us and were pleased with our action,” he said. The difference in the WCK incident was that foreign nationals were killed, he said. “That’s the whole difference. Not a substantive difference.”
When the WCK convoy was destroyed, it was nowhere near Israeli troops. Several Israeli officers familiar with the incident said the strikes were not ordered on the basis of an imminent threat to Israeli lives, but to fulfil the mission to thwart Hamas attempts to control aid deliveries.
An IDF statement said the airstrikes were a result of an “erroneous assessment that Hamas military operatives were present in the vehicles, rather than from an intention to target the organisation’s personnel”.
The statement added that “this assessment was compounded by serious failures to comply with applicable orders and procedures”. However, it said: “Following an in-depth examination of the findings and in light of the standards applicable under criminal law, it was determined that, despite the aforementioned failures, the circumstances of the incident did not give rise to a reasonable suspicion of a criminal offence warranting the opening of a criminal investigation.”
The WCK said the Israeli decision not to pursue criminal proceedings was “inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive”. “At the time of the lethal attacks, our team in Gaza was unarmed and posing a threat to nobody,” the WCK said. “The IDF had full visual clarity on our clearly marked humanitarian vehicles during the extended, multiple airstrikes. It knew our team’s movements, identities and activities in advance.”
Britain, Australia and Canada denounced the prosecutor’s decision as “shameful”, saying they would “continue to seek answers” on behalf of the slain aid workers. The UK opened an inquest in 2024 into the deaths of the three British team members: James Kirby, James Henderson and John Chapman.
Saifeddin Abutaha, a Palestinian, Australian Zomi Frankcom, Damian Sobol, a Pole, and a dual Canadian-US citizen, Jacob Flickinger, were the other victims. The UK inquest was adjourned pending the outcome of the Israeli investigation.
Mendel, who is the only officer of such high rank to have been dismissed for his actions in the Gaza war, has been portrayed in army command briefings as a rogue operator. Questions have been raised about a political motive. Mendel is a settler who is reported to have been one of the 130 signatories of a 20 January 2024 letter to the IDF calling for the flow of aid to Gaza to be restricted.
However, the way the Israeli army operates in Gaza – rules of engagement are made contingent on local circumstances and passed on, often verbally, down the chain of command – gives officers at Mendel’s level wide discretion in subjective judgments as to who is a “terrorist” and therefore a target.
The IDF statement said its activity in the Gaza Strip was “regulated by a broad range of binding written orders and standing directives governing the use of force, the approval processes for strikes, strikes against sensitive sites, and other matters” and that these incorporated “the rules of the laws of armed conflict, including the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precautions in attack”.
The statement said that “a person does not become a lawful target merely because they are in the vicinity of an armed individual, come into contact with them, or travel alongside them”.
The IDF said: “Carrying a weapon may be a relevant factor in such an assessment, but is not sufficient on its own without meeting the definitions described above. In particular, and in the context of the incident in question, security personnel hired to protect a humanitarian convoy from looting do not become lawful targets merely because they are armed.”
An IDF officer familiar with the WCK killings said that given the circumstances and the standing IDF procedures, the overwhelming majority of officers would have acted in the same way. “There were armed men next to them,” the officer said. “If you took qualified people and put them on the call, in 90% of cases this is what would have happened,” the officer said. “In my guess, 99% of the time the first bomb would have been dropped; 90% of the time the second; 80% of the time the third.”
Reserve Brigadier General Oren Solomon, the battle manager of Gaza Division, said that a mistake had been made in determining that an armed man had entered one of the vehicles, but added that once that error had been committed, the incrimination procedure led inevitably to the three missile strikes.
“If I incriminated this vehicle beforehand as Hamas – anyone who escapes from it and enters another vehicle: death comes,” Brig Gen Solomon said. “Together with him they will die. That meets the incrimination rules, no problem.”
A senior officer involved in the initial Israeli military investigation into the WCK case, argued Mendel overstepped in interpreting the rules of incrimination.
“You can’t incriminate 20 people if there’s one armed,” he said. The officer argued that the first strike could have been justified by the initial misidentification, even at the cost of civilian casualties, but not the subsequent missiles.
“You struck someone you suspected, a vehicle you suspected had an armed man in it. The moment two people came out, nobody with a weapon, the second and third strikes are contrary to orders because you don’t know whom you’re striking,” he said.
The other systemic factor that contributed to the deaths of the seven aid workers, and potentially countless more civilians, was one of the missions given to the army in Gaza by Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition government: to destroy Hamas’s influence and control. That meant anyone deemed to be involved in – or assisting – the Hamas administration, including by distributing aid, could find themselves in the sights of an Israeli drone operator.
“I remind you that part of our mission was to crush Hamas’s ability to govern,” Mendel said. “Part of the mission was to hit that [Hamas-controlled aid deliveries], and we hit it.””
Interviews with IDF officers suggest there was a widespread belief in the ranks that Hamas had wrested control of the bulk of aid deliveries into Gaza. That assumption was unfounded, later analysis showed. It was a period of widespread hunger caused by an Israeli blockade, when food convoys were being mobbed by desperate civilians, criminal gangs and Hamas militia.
The belief that Hamas hijacks were widespread meant that the appearance of armed men in proximity to the WCK vehicle in April 2024 fitted a “pattern of activity” that helped incriminate the whole convoy in the eyes of Mendel and his unit.
The IDF officer familiar with the incident said it was common practice to designate any armed man in Gaza as Hamas or a “terrorist”, as Mendel did. The officer added: “How you define that it’s Hamas – he’s in proximity to weapons, and because he touches the trucks, and because he does all sorts of things that look as if he’s going to take over the trucks.”
The role of the incrimination principle in the WCK killings shows how it has become a factor in the historically high proportion of civilians killed in the Gaza war. This sits alongside the routine acceptance of high “collateral damage” in the targeting of Hamas militants, the designation of large and shifting areas as free-fire zones, and the deliberate levelling of neighbourhoods to prevent the return of Palestinian communities.
The common factor is that constraints on targeting were minimised in the interests of an open-ended mission. Since the start of the war in 2023, no Israeli soldier has been convicted of wrongful death or war crimes in Gaza operations.
“I came to defeat Hamas,” Mendel said. “If such an event came before me again, I would do exactly the same thing.”
He also dismissed the significance of the killings. “I think it’s an idiotic side event,” Mendel said. “It really isn’t a serious event.”

articles.title: Advanced enemy technology failed to shield aircraft from indigenous air defenses
articles.body:
Advanced enemy technology failed to shield aircraft from indigenous air defenses
TEHRAN — Iran’s air defense commander says the country’s recent experience of war has demonstrated that technological superiority alone cannot guarantee the safety of an attacking force, stating that Iranian forces developed and upgraded new domestically produced air defense systems even as the fighting was underway.
Brigadier General Alireza Elhami, commander of Khatam al-Anbiya Joint Air Defense Headquarters and the Army’s Air Defense Force, made the remarks on Friday.
Elhami said Iran had relied on “100-percent Iranian capabilities” during the recent conflict, identifying courageous leadership, national cohesion and public support as three of the principal pillars of the country’s wartime resilience.
He said Iranian defense personnel had developed and manufactured air defense systems during the conflict, subsequently deploying them to operational areas where, according to his account, they were used against hostile aircraft.
“Advanced enemy technology did not provide them with immunity,” Elhami said, arguing that even highly sophisticated aircraft entering the battlefield could not be assured of a safe return.
His comments were consistent with a report published Friday by Tasnim, which said Iran’s Army air defense force had achieved self-sufficiency in supplying the weapons, equipment and defense systems it requires by relying on domestic expertise, knowledge-based companies and universities.
Elhami said the Iranian air defense industry was increasingly drawing on young defense scientists, domestic technology companies, universities and operational experience accumulated during the war.
He also warned that, in Iran’s assessment, the conflict was not necessarily over and that the armed forces needed to remain prepared for 'new threats and fronts.'
US and Israel failed to achieve objectives
Separately, Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia, spokesman for Iran’s Army, said the United States and Israel had failed to achieve the objectives they had pursued during their latest military campaign against Iran.
Speaking at an event in Mashhad on Friday, Akraminia said the adversary had entered the conflict after making a series of miscalculations about Iran, including its society, military capabilities and political structure.
He added that the attackers had sought to degrade Iran’s missile and nuclear capabilities, overthrow its government and ultimately partition the country. “None of these objectives was achieved,” he said.
Akraminia also cited 'a failure by the United States and its Western allies' to build a broader military coalition against Iran.
He said the confrontation had become a test of political and national will as much as military capability, arguing that Iran’s religious beliefs, social resilience and experience from previous conflicts had strengthened its ability to withstand pressure.
Iran announces further strikes on US bases
Against that backdrop, Iran’s Army said it had continued its missile and drone operations against US military positions in the region.
In a statement, the Army said Iranian forces had struck satellite communications systems, equipment storage facilities and fighter aircraft shelters at Ahmad al-Jaber Air Base in Kuwait.
The Iranian military also said missile and one-way attack drone strikes had targeted troop positions and radar systems at Al Minhad Air Base in the United Arab Emirates.
Iran said the attacks caused damage to communications infrastructure and aircraft shelters.
The two bases are important components of the US military presence in the Persian Gulf. Ahmad al-Jaber is a significant US air facility in Kuwait, while Al Minhad has served as an important hub for air operations and the movement of foreign forces in the region.

articles.title: Russia Continues Missile and Drone Strikes on Ukraine Amid Reports of Possible Suspension of Ukrainian Attacks
articles.body:
On the night of September 5, Russian troops continued to strike Ukraine with missiles and drone-launched rockets, following a statement by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky regarding a possible suspension of Ukrainian long-range strikes during the visit to Moscow by special envoys of U.S. President Trump.
This is evidenced by data from the Ukrainian Air Force and local authorities.
After midnight in the city of Boryspil of the Kyiv region a Russian drone struck the roof of a nine-story residential building.
The strike caused a fire and damage to the roof and to one of the apartments on the top floor.
Later, Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, reported that two women were injured and hospitalized with various injuries.
The Russians also struck the city of Kamianske in the Dnipropetrovsk region with several ballistic missiles.
The Regional Military Administration reported that the target of the missile strikes was an industrial facility. By morning, it was reported that four people had been killed and five wounded as a result of this attack.
“Three of the victims are in the hospital. Among them is a 30-year-old woman who is in intensive care. Medical personnel are providing the wounded with all necessary care,” said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional administration.
On the evening of September 4, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that during the visits of U.S. President Donald Trump’s special representatives, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, to Moscow and Kyiv, Ukraine would ensure the “normal functioning of Russian airspace.”
“And just as we did during previous diplomatic visits by the U.S. side, we will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace so that the negotiators can arrive safely. We are looking out for them, not for Russia,” Zelensky said.
The president noted that while negotiations are underway and logistical issues related to the U.S. delegation’s visit are being resolved, Ukraine will not carry out airstrikes. At the same time, he said, Russia must reciprocally ensure a cessation of airstrikes during this period. Axios reported yesterday that visits by Trump’s special envoys will take place this weekend.
The Ukrainian Armed Forces have also been ordered to observe a ceasefire along the front lines from 12:00 a.m. on September 5 to 11:59 p.m. on September 8.

articles.body:
Kyrylo Budanov, head of the Office of the President of Ukraine, stated on Saturday, Sept. 5, that Russia failed to respond to a proposed ceasefire intended to coincide with the visit of US diplomatic envoys to Moscow and Kyiv.
In a comment to the Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne, Budanov said the proposal was communicated directly to Russian President Vladimir Putin. The initiative called for a temporary halt to both aerial strikes and frontline combat operations.

Addressing the lack of a Russian response and the continuation of hostilities, Budanov noted that Russian drones continue to strike Ukrainian territory.

Combat continues following rejected truce

The General Staff of the AFU stated that a unilateral ceasefire is impossible due to the operational risk it poses to military personnel, adding that defensive tasks are continuing according to plan.
The Russian Ministry of Defense confirmed its refusal to observe the temporary truce, publishing a report detailing its overnight combined strikes across Ukraine.
Combat Continues as Russia Rejects Ceasefire
These overnight operations included a ballistic missile strike on an industrial enterprise in Kamianske, Dnipropetrovsk region, that killed five people and injured five others.
Concurrently, Russian forces launched consecutive drone strikes on an Epicenter shopping center in Mykolaiv, injuring two civilians and triggering a large fire.

articles.title: Iran's seven islands strengthen Hormuz control
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
The seven islands: what we know about Iran's maritime line controlling Hormuz
As Iran continues to keep the Strait of Hormuz closed, the question is no longer limited to the impact of the closure on global energy markets and the economy.
It has shifted to uncovering the mechanisms Iran uses to control what is currently the world's most sensitive shipping route.
This does not refer to Iran's military capabilities but rather to a complex network of strategic islands whose function Iran has reshaped, turning them into "fixed aircraft carriers" through which it controls shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.
Geographically, the Strait of Hormuz, located south of Hormozgan province, forms a natural boundary between Iran and Oman.
It is a narrow passage constrained by navigational challenges. Strong water currents and varying depths force giant tankers to follow specific and extremely narrow routes, increasing Tehran's ability to control and monitor them.
The area derives its strategic importance from being the world's second-busiest strait, with about 17 million barrels of crude oil passing through it every day.
This represents 40% of oil transported by sea and about 25% of total global supplies, in a region that alone holds 68% of the world's proven oil and gas reserves.
Characteristics of the Strait of Hormuz
The Strait of Hormuz is estimated to be 167 kilometres long, while its width varies depending on the area.
It reaches about 95 kilometres at its widest point and narrows to about 33 kilometres at its narrowest.
However, official shipping lanes are much narrower. Each lane designated for vessel traffic is no more than 3 kilometres wide, with a buffer zone separating the inbound and outbound lanes.
The depth of the Strait of Hormuz also varies, reaching more than 60 metres in some areas, while ranging between 30 and 40 metres in shallow areas.
Although this depth is suitable for giant oil tankers and heavy vessels, it forces large ships to follow specific and limited routes, increasing the area's security importance.
The narrowest point of the strait is 21 nautical miles wide, located between Iran's Larak Island and Oman's Greater Quoin Island.
Until 1979, shipping traffic followed the shortest route between the Quoin and Musandam islands.
That year, Oman announced that vessels should pass through an area outside the range of Quoin Island in order to reduce security risks to routes near its islands and territory.
For about 60 years, the shipping route in the Strait of Hormuz passed through Iranian territorial waters.
But Tehran rejected this after it was subjected to war and closed the strait, announcing the opening of a northern route for vessels after they obtained permission from the Iranian navy.
Iran has also held negotiations in recent weeks with Oman to establish a new shipping route.
An agreement was reached, although it was not announced. However, Iranian authorities continue to refuse to reopen the Strait of Hormuz without a response from Washington to its conditions for ending the war permanently, lifting the blockade and sanctions, releasing its frozen assets and other demands.
An island shield to retain Hormuz
Iran's ability to control the Strait of Hormuz is not limited to its coastal capabilities stretching for about 160 kilometres.
A group of Iranian islands also plays a vital role in strengthening this control within these waters.
These islands have given Iran a unique geopolitical position at the entrance to the Gulf, allowing it to control the strait and traffic passing through it.
Seven islands form Iran's curved defensive line in the area for controlling shipping traffic: Hormuz, Larak, Qeshm, Hengam, Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb and Abu Musa.
The last three islands are disputed between Iran and the United Arab Emirates but are currently under Iranian control.
Four of these islands are located at the entrance to the strait — Hormuz, Qeshm, Larak and Hengam — while the other three disputed islands lie west of this curved line.
The short distances between these islands and the depth of the waters in this area force warships and oil tankers to pass close to them when entering the Strait of Hormuz.
This currently exposes these vessels to threats from fast boats, mines or drones stationed on the islands.
These islands are so important to Iran that former Iranian navigation official Ali Ezzati described them in a statement as "fixed aircraft carriers that cannot be sunk".
The seven islands
1 — Hormuz Island
The island is about 8 kilometres wide and is located 20 kilometres south of Bandar Abbas port.
Over the past centuries, Hormuz has been regarded as the key to entering the Gulf. The naming of the strait after it is evidence of this status.
The island is oval-shaped, covering about 42 square kilometres along the strait, and is a tourist destination in southern Iran.
Hormuz City is located in the north and is the island's only population centre. Its population stood at 5,891 according to the 2016 census.
It was under Portuguese occupation for more than a century before Iran regained control of it in 1622 under Shah Abbas.
The Iranian Achaemenid Empire used the island as a naval base more than 2,500 years ago.
Throughout history, it served as a commercial meeting point for traders from India, China and other eastern markets.
The Portuguese viewed it as an impregnable fortress overlooking the meeting point between the Gulf waters and the Indian Ocean.
In the modern era, which has seen the passage of giant oil tankers, Hormuz Island has retained its strategic position despite its relative distance from the deep-water shipping channel.
2 — Larak Island
Larak is located 40 kilometres south of Bandar Abbas, the centre of Hormozgan province, 20 kilometres west of Hormuz Island and 12 kilometres east of Qeshm Island.
Larak is unique in being the Iranian island directly adjacent to the deep-water channel in the Strait of Hormuz that is suitable for the passage of giant oil tankers.
Since Iran announced the closure of the Strait of Hormuz following the US-Israeli war on 28 February, Larak has been closely linked to developments involving the shipping route.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps launched an alternative route for shipping through Iranian territorial waters, bypassing the historic route that passed through Omani waters.
The new Iranian route passes south of Larak Island, overlooking the vital energy corridor, making its location the main pillar of Tehran's military system aimed at retaining control over the Strait of Hormuz.
The island lies at the easternmost point of the Gulf and is administratively part of Iran's Hormozgan province.
It is oval-shaped and extends 10.5 kilometres from northeast to southwest.
3 — Qeshm Island
Qeshm is the largest island in the Gulf, with an area twice that of Bahrain, which is the second-largest island in the region.
Qeshm is located 20 kilometres south of Bandar Abbas, 40 kilometres east of Bandar Lengeh and 31 kilometres east of Greater Tunb.
It is 140 kilometres long.
Qeshm is characterised by its sandy terrain, with hills spread across its central areas.
The highest point is Mount Buko, which rises 405 metres above sea level.
The island covers 1,644 square kilometres and is rich in natural resources, including oil, gas, lead, sulphur and salts.
The island had a population of 148,993 in the 2016 census, with 66,801 living in urban areas and 82,160 in villages and towns.
Over the past decade, Qeshm has become a prominent tourist destination because of its environment and natural and historical sites.
Parts of it have been part of the Global Geoparks Network under the auspices of UNESCO since 2006, as the first geopark in the Middle East.
4 — Hengam Island
Hengam is located just 3 kilometres south of Qeshm Island.
It is about 50 kilometres from Oman's Ghanam Island and shares with Larak Island direct oversight of the deep edge of the shipping routes in the Strait of Hormuz.
The island contains scattered population centres across an area of about 50 square kilometres south of Qeshm.
It contains deposits of salt, soil and lead.
It is 10 kilometres long and between 3 and 6 kilometres wide.
During the Qajar monarchy, Britain established facilities and military bases on the island.
Hengam's coastline is suitable for deploying fleets and naval vessels because of the deep waters surrounding its shores, making it suitable as a berth for warships and submarines.
Its location in the middle of the Gulf waters, adjacent to the Strait of Hormuz and Qeshm, has given it major strategic and military importance.
This has made it historically vulnerable to attempts at control by successive foreign powers.
It was occupied by the Portuguese during the Safavid era and later by the British during the Qajar period.
5 — Greater Tunb
Greater Tunb is one of three islands disputed between Iran and the UAE.
It lies 31 kilometres southwest of Qeshm Island and faces the Strait of Hormuz to the west.
The island is one of the main pillars of Tehran's defence and military doctrine for protecting and managing the strait.
The island is 12 kilometres from Lesser Tunb, 50 kilometres from Abu Musa and about 82 kilometres from Al Hamra Island in Ras Al Khaimah.
It lies north of the Gulf's median line and is roughly circular, covering about 12 square kilometres.
It is predominantly dry and sandy, with little vegetation, while hills in the north reach a maximum height of 53 metres.
6 — Lesser Tunb
Lesser Tunb is the other disputed island between Tehran and Abu Dhabi.
It lies on the northern side of the Gulf's median line, 12 kilometres from Greater Tunb, 50 kilometres from Bandar Lengeh and 92 kilometres from the coast of Ras Al Khaimah in the UAE.
The island covers only about 2 square kilometres, which explains the name "Lesser".
It is roughly triangular in shape, with a width ranging between 1,100 and 1,500 metres.
A dark rocky hill rises 35 metres above sea level in its northwestern part.
Its shores are steep, amid a hot and humid climate, and it has no fresh water.
Unlike Greater Tunb, it is uninhabited and is predominantly used for military and security purposes related to protection and surveillance.
Its spread of rocks and salt domes gives it rugged terrain.
7 — Abu Musa
Abu Musa is the third island disputed between Iran and the UAE.
It forms the westernmost point of Iran's maritime defensive arc and is the final link in the Iranian defence system stationed at the Gulf's gateway.
It is 67 kilometres from Bandar Lengeh and 62 kilometres from Sharjah port in the UAE.
The island has an airport and a seaport, with regular flights operating between it and Bandar Abbas.
There are also passenger sea transport services using boats and vessels departing from Bandar Lengeh two to three times a week.
Its area is larger than that of both Greater Tunb and Lesser Tunb.
It has an irregular shape, while its central and southern areas are flat and sandy.
Its oil resources are limited to the Mubarak field, located offshore to the east of the island.
Its oil is classified as among the highest-quality crude extracted in the Gulf basin.
Revolutionary Guard Navy responsible for security
According to Iran's naval military divisions and formations, the first and fifth naval regions of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy are responsible for securing this curved defensive line and its surrounding area in the Strait of Hormuz.
The First Naval Region, known as "Sahib al-Zaman", is one of the five naval regions of the Revolutionary Guard.
It operates under the supervision of the naval force and the "Khatam al-Anbiya 2" naval headquarters.
The command headquarters of this region is located in Bandar Abbas.
It is the formation closest to the Strait of Hormuz and is responsible for conducting defensive and offensive operations in the area of the passage.
Rear Adm. Abbas Gholamshahi commands it.
On 4 November 2012, the Revolutionary Guard Navy established its Fifth Naval Region, named "Imam Mohammad Baqer", in Bandar Lengeh, overlooking the Gulf waters west of the Strait of Hormuz.
It assigned the region responsibility for controlling the area extending from the end of Qeshm Island, through an area of four islands that became known militarily as the "Naz'at" islands, to the west of Kish Island.
Under this military division, protection and security of the Strait of Hormuz itself was assigned to the First Naval Region as a direct naval mission.
The Fifth Naval Region, meanwhile, was independently tasked with protecting and securing the "Naz'at" island system in the western extension of the Strait of Hormuz.
The four defensive Naz'at islands are Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb, Abu Musa and Siri Island.
Tehran relies on a diverse and hybrid arsenal to close or obstruct shipping through this strategic passage.
It combines coastal and mobile weapons along the coast and islands, ranging from underground missile cities and naval and coastal anti-ship missile launchers to fast boats, attack drones and naval mines capable of blocking the route of giant tankers.
Iran also relies on military capabilities beyond its coasts and islands, in both its missile and drone capacities, to tighten its control over the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian army spokesman Mohammad Akram Nia previously said that "Iran can establish control over the Strait of Hormuz from any point on its territory".
