articles.title: Qatar rejects Iran claim strikes only targeted US military sites
articles.body:
Qatar said on Friday that official records it submitted to the UN show Iranian missiles struck civilian, commercial and residential areas in the country, rejecting Tehran’s attempt to cite a Qatari document as evidence that its attacks were limited to US military facilities. 
Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed Al-Ansari made the remarks in a statement responding to a post on US social media company X by Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei. 
Baghaei cited a safety and security risk assessment prepared by Qatar for the ITU Plenipotentiary Conference, claiming the document confirmed that Iranian strikes exclusively targeted US military facilities in Qatar and did not target civilian areas, except for gas facilities in Ras Laffan that he alleged were being used in US military operations against Iran. 
Qatar hosts the Al Udeid Air Base, which houses the Combined Air Operations Center responsible for command and control of air operations across the US military’s Central Command area of responsibility, as well as a forward headquarters for the command, according to US military information. 
“If the Iranian side wishes to reference official documentation, we invite it to refer to the record formally submitted by the State of Qatar to the United Nations, rather than selectively quoting a security risk assessment prepared for operational purposes,” Al-Ansari said. 
“Qatar’s identical letters dated 1 March 2026 (S/2026/110) documented the launch of Iranian missiles over civilian, commercial and residential areas, resulting in damage and injuries to 16 people. Qatar’s letter dated 20 July also documented further attacks that injured three people, including a child,” he added. 
The attacks came amid the war that erupted on Feb. 28, when the US and Israel launched large-scale military strikes against Iran, followed by Iranian attacks on Israel and countries across the region, including Qatar. 
On the same day, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned the US and Israeli strikes on Iran, as well as subsequent Iranian attacks that he said violated the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Qatar, Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
Since the beginning of the war, Qatar has sent letters to the UN and the Security Council documenting Iranian attacks on its territory. 
“The document now being cited by the Iranian side is a safety and security risk assessment prepared for the ITU Plenipotentiary Conference. It is neither a comprehensive factual record nor a legal assessment of the events,” said Al-Ansari. 
“In fact, it expressly acknowledges direct attacks inside the State of Qatar, including the 18 March attack on gas facilities in Ras Laffan, and refers to the temporary closure of Qatari airspace and the impact on civilian life. Selectively extracting a sentence from that document while disregarding its broader context is therefore misleading.”  
Al-Ansari said the success of Qatar Armed Forces in intercepting Iranian missiles and drones “does not diminish the gravity of these attacks, nor does it absolve those responsible of accountability.” 
“It is regrettable that the attack on Ras Laffan has been described as ‘alleged,’ despite having been formally documented in Qatar’s letter S/2026/207, particularly given that these facilities are national assets belonging to the Qatari people and form an integral part of the global energy security architecture,” he said. 
In the letter, Qatar told the Security Council that Iran launched seven ballistic missiles toward Ras Laffan Industrial City on March 18, with Qatari forces intercepting six while one missile struck the city, causing fires and significant damage. The area came under another missile attack in the early hours of the following day. 
Qatar said in the note that it had “distanced itself from this war from its outset” and sought to avoid becoming involved in the escalation, accusing Iran of continuing to target Qatari territory and neighboring countries. 
“The State of Qatar is not a party to this conflict. Attacks on its territory and civilian infrastructure, the endangerment of its population, and destabilizing actions in the Strait of Hormuz cannot be justified as ‘legitimate responses,’” said Al-Ansari. “Such acts constitute clear violations of international law, and no selective quotation or interpretation can alter that fact.” 
The exchange between Qatar and Iran comes amid renewed escalation between Washington and Tehran, with the two trading military strikes in early September in one of the fiercest rounds of escalation since July, while shipping through the Strait of Hormuz continues to be affected. 
“Guided by its longstanding position that dialogue and peaceful means remain the best path to resolving differences, Qatar will continue its diplomatic efforts and sustained endeavors to de-escalate tensions and promote security and stability in the region,” the Qatari spokesman said. 
Letters to UN, Security Council rep. 
In the letters sent to Guterres and France’s UN representative Jerome Bonnafont, who is holding the rotating presidency of the Security Council, Qatar rejected Iranian claims regarding recent territorial attacks, asserting its right to self-defense and compensation.
 The letters said Iranian claims cannot provide a legal basis for “unjustified and unlawful” attacks against Qatar. Doha argued that the strikes violate international law and UN Charter Article 2(4), which prohibits the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state. Qatar also cited UN Security Council Resolution 2817, which previously condemned the attacks as threats to international peace. 
Doha also dismissed Iran's invocation of Article 51 self-defense and pointed out that Tehran's reliance on the 1974 UN General Assembly definition of aggression actually undermines its own position. The letters noted that the definition explicitly considers the bombardment of another state's territory and the blockade of ports, referencing Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz, as acts of aggression. 
Qatar accused Tehran of targeting critical civilian infrastructure, including energy facilities, oil tankers, and commercial vessels in violation of the Geneva Conventions.

articles.title: Ukraine says 4 killed, 7 injured in Russian overnight strikes
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
05 September 2026•Update: 05 September 2026
Four people were killed and seven others injured in overnight Russian strikes on Ukraine, Ukrainian officials said Saturday.
In the Dnipropetrovsk region, Russia struck an industrial enterprise in Kamianske, killing four people and injuring five others, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Telegram.
In the Kyiv region, two people were injured in an attack on Boryspil, Governor Timur Tkachenko said on Telegram.
Tkachenko said efforts were underway to assess and address the consequences of the strike on a nine-story residential building.
The Ukrainian Air Force said on Telegram that 128 Russian drones were shot down overnight.
Meanwhile, Russia's Defense Ministry said that its forces struck two of Ukraine's largest suppliers of metal products for the military in the Dnipropetrovsk region.
The ministry said Russian forces also struck logistics centers, a dry cargo ship, two fuel storage and distribution facilities and an electronic intelligence center in the Mykolaiv, Odesa and Kyiv regions.
It also said Russian air defenses intercepted and destroyed 53 Ukrainian drones across Russia, annexed Crimea and over the Black Sea.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Friday that Kyiv “will ensure the normal functioning of Russian airspace” during an expected visit to Moscow by US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
“We are looking out for them, not for Russia,” Zelenskyy wrote on US social media platform X.
“There will be no air strikes from our side, and Russia must do the same, ensuring there are no air strikes from its side for the time needed to hold these talks and handle the logistical matters related to this American visit,” he added.
 
Axios news website and Russian state news agency Tass reported, citing sources, that the two US envoys will visit Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend.
Witkoff and Kushner have never visited Kyiv, while both have made several trips to Moscow since US-mediated talks began.
Their latest visit was on Jan. 22, when they met Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin.

articles.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy accuses Russia of 'demonstrative strikes' on Kiev airports amid US envoys' visit
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Saturday accused Russia of carrying out “demonstrative strikes” on airports in Kiev and Boryspil overnight ahead of a planned visit to the Ukrainian capital by US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner.
“Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the US side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kiev Airport or Boryspil Airport,” Zelenskyy wrote on the US social media platform X.
He said Moscow had deliberately targeted the airports “for the first time in a while”.
“Russian-Iranian ‘shaheds’ in response to American diplomacy,” he said.
“We have taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky.”
Zelenskyy said Kiev would not allow threats to undermine diplomacy on its part, stressing that Ukraine was interested in bringing peace closer.
“Russia will be held accountable for what it does,” he added.
Witkoff, Kushner in Moscow
Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Moscow on Saturday for talks aimed at ending the Russia-Ukraine war, Russian state news agency TASS reported.
According to the agency, a special jet carrying the two US envoys landed at Vnukovo Airport.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev arrived at the airport to meet the American representatives, the agency reported.
Zelenskyy said Witkoff and Kushner would visit Kiev on Sunday following their trip to Moscow.
Neither envoy has previously visited Kiev, although both have made several trips to Moscow since US-mediated talks began.
Their latest visit was on January 22, when they met Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin.
Meanwhile, five people were killed and five others wounded in Ukrainian strikes over the past 24 hours in the Russian-controlled part of Ukraine's Luhansk region, Leonid Pasechnik, the Russian governor, said on Saturday.

articles.title: Europe would not be able to sustain war of attrition with Russia, defence officials say
articles.body:
Defence planners working with Nato fear that if war broke out with Russia, Europe could not currently sustain a prolonged war of attrition owing to a public lack of war readiness, a conference on the future of European military coordination heard this week.
The pessimism reflects concern that Russia may be winning a so-called hybrid war with Europe, weakening the options available to Nato war planners in the event of military conflict.
The surge in support for the populist forces in Europe’s main military states is also endangering proposals for a group of five European countries, including the UK, to take on a new coordination role as the US prepares to reduce its commitments to the conventional defence of Europe.
Defence officials, speaking at a forum convened by the Munich Security Conference (MSC), the leading security foundation, said the European public may not have the appetite for a prolonged war, requiring Nato to focus its plans on a relatively quick conflict.
One recent British cabinet member admitted the west had been “crap” at educating its public about the scale of the hybrid conflict with Russia. Another UK diplomat claimed successive British prime ministers had done nothing to explain the scale of the threat.
They said this had left ministers locked in an unenviable task of persuading unprepared voters to cut welfare spending to fund defence. “The level of the debate has been at that of a kindergarten,” the UK diplomat admitted.
The private criticism has been fuelled by the UK government’s inability to adopt a call in its 2025 strategic defence review to launch a national conversation on the scale of the security threat facing Europe and to build national resilience.
A second diplomat said the collapse of the cold war dividing line with Russia had left Moscow free to exploit the anxieties of European publics on the left and the right. The remarks reveal a wider concern in senior European politicians that they may be losing the so-called hybrid war with Russia, and this may be reflected in rightwing populist surges next year in Poland, France and Italy.
Most populist parties, including Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), are sympathetic to Russia and want an end to the Ukraine conflict.
The MSC discussion – held under rules forbidding identification of the speaker – was given added urgency by the German government this week blaming Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig airport last month.
One of the suspected culprits in the attack on 4 August, where an armed drone exploded, has been identified as a Belarusian citizen with a Russian passport who appears to have entered Europe using an Italian tourist visa.
The MSC, an independent but influential foundation, has been promoting the idea of the five main European military powers working much more closely: one means of bringing the UK, outside the EU, to the centre of European defence planning.
Decisions in Washington on its troop deployments that could effectively leave Europe in charge of its own conventional defences are expected in the next few months. But the scale of hybrid war and the potential impact of next year’s elections, as well as the surge by the AfD in Germany, on plans for a stronger European defence coordination was described at the conference as “the elephant in the room”.
One proposal is for the EU to publish a collective statement on the Russian threat that the populist forces would be challenged to accept or decline.
The E5 group of European defence ministers already meet regularly, but they are at the early stages of agreeing of how to jointly procure capabilities such as integrated air and missile defence, deep precision strike and space-based early warning systems that are all currently provided mostly by the US.
“Europe is stagnating at a time when the external threats were assuming a dimension which is really very serious. These are really huge and existential challenges requiring greater integration in defence,” said Wolfgang Ischinger, the chair of the MSC.
He argued the E5 grouping offers a way of including all the European countries with substantial defence industrial capacity and may later be able to incorporate Ukraine in the context of a truce since Kyiv now has the largest and strongest army in Europe.
Advocates of the E5 insist it will neither duplicate nor underline Nato, but fears were expressed that the US would nevertheless block a stronger European pillar inside Nato. “The US are better at talking about burden shifting than power sharing,” said one diplomat.
Italy is one of the E5 states most concerned about the impact of Russia’s hybrid warfare on its domestic politics as Giorgia Meloni’s rightwing administration – which has governed more moderately than many expected, and cultivated a pro-Ukraine image abroad – becomes its longest-running since the second world war.
The Italian foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, warned Italy was suffering daily cyber-attacks, adding it was not immune from potential Russian interference in next year’s national elections, the first time an Italian politicians has warned the election may be manipulated.
“There are many ways to wage hybrid warfare, it is not done using bombs, planes or tanks,” the minister said.
Italy’s defence minister, Guido Crosetto, one of Meloni’s closest political allies, has said it was stupid not to recognise the level of Russian interference.
He warned this summer at the Nato summit in Ankara: “We don’t have the antibodies and we’re penetrable: analyse bots and you’ll see it. The increase occurred thanks to social media.”
His doubts have grown given Moscow’s ability to operate across so many domains, including social media, AI, cybersecurity, databases and critical infrastructure. On Tuesday, he said the Russian threat was growing all the time.
Crosetto also said he recognises Russia is exploiting real problems such as low wages, and so attributing government unpopularity to Russian disinformation risks misidentifying a malaise afflicting western societies, including a general weariness with the cost of the war in Ukraine,
In Italy, Roberto Vannacci, the leader of the far-right Futuro Nazionale who has challenged the stability of Meloni’s coalition, is widely seen as the most probable carrier of the Russian message in the coming election, that could come as early as April.
Speaking before the investigation into whether his party represents a revival of fascism, Vannacci gloried in the criticism. “Just discovered that I am a ‘Manchurian candidate’ sent by the Russian federation to complain about the unaffordable petrol prices in my country Italy,” he said. “Forgive me, but I still find it hard to accept the idea that dissent from Brussels’ orthodoxy is now, in practical terms, tantamount to disloyalty towards the west.”
In an attempt to shift perceptions so Ukraine is seen not as a financial burden but rather as teaching Europe modern warfare, Crosetto has recruited the former Ukraine defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov as his unpaid adviser for innovation. Ischinger praised the decision, describing Ukraine as possessing the best equipped and most modern army in Europe.
In Ukraine, 200,000 drones are being built each month, with the goal of producing more than 7m by 2026. To support this growth, 500 small and medium-sized companies have sprung up, assembling drones even in small workshops, using mostly Chinese components.

articles.title: SBU exposes Russian spy operating within Ukrainian Armed Forces in Kharkiv
articles.body:
SBU exposes Russian spy operating within Ukrainian Armed Forces in Kharkiv
The SBU said this in a statement seen by Ukrinform.
One of those detained is a local man who was mobilized into a Ukrainian Territorial Defense brigade. He was working for Russian military intelligence, better known as the GRU, and was passing information to the enemy from "inside" the Ukrainian military.
The investigation established that Russian intelligence recruited the Kharkiv resident through his neighbor, a professor at a Kharkiv university whom the SBU exposed in March this year for adjusting Russian strikes on the city.
After the university lecturer was detained, the suspect, acting on orders from the enemy, joined the Ukrainian military, where he was assigned as a reserve soldier in a reserve company of a combat unit.
There, under the guise of official trips, the agent monitored the locations of Ukrainian air defense and electronic warfare units, as well as defensive fortifications around Kharkiv.
He also marked the locations of local combined heat and power plants and key electrical substations supplying the city and surrounding areas on Google Maps.
The suspect later recruited his unemployed wife to cooperate with the enemy. Initially, she walked around the city to identify locations where Ukrainian troops were based and passed the intelligence to her husband. She later reported directly to her Russian handler.
The man's next assignment was to undergo training as an unmanned systems operator and hand over to Russian intelligence materials obtained during the training.
After completing the courses, the serviceman hoped to receive a promotion to a position in a UAV unit, which would allow him to expand his espionage activities in favor of the aggressor state.
SBU officers exposed the agent couple, documented their criminal activities step by step and detained both suspects: the man during another intelligence-gathering mission and his wife at their place of residence.
During searches, investigators seized 12 smartphones, four laptops and two tablets, which the suspects regularly switched in order to maintain covert communications with the Russian GRU.
SBU investigators notified both detainees that they were suspected of violating Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – high treason committed under martial law.
The suspects are being held in custody without the right to bail. They face life imprisonment with confiscation of property.

articles.title: Rights organizations demand Congress scrap US-Israel military integration bill
articles.body:
Rights organizations demand Congress scrap US-Israel military integration bill
TEHRAN — 56 American civil rights and advocacy organizations have issued a blunt demand to Congress: strip a controversial provision from the 2027 National Defense Authorization Act or risk permanently entrenching Israel inside the Pentagon’s core technology apparatus.
In a joint letter sent to leaders of the House and Senate Armed Services Committees, the coalition warned that the legislation creates dangerous points of foreign leverage at a moment when American public support for Israel has collapsed following its brutal campaigns of regional aggression.
Designated Section 219 in the House draft and Section 1217 in the Senate version, the proposal establishes the United States-Israel Defense Technology Cooperation Initiative.
Moving far beyond traditional foreign aid packages subject to yearly congressional debate, the mandate legally enforces co-production plants, joint weapons development, and data fusion across artificial intelligence, cyber warfare, and autonomous systems.
Signatories including Amnesty International USA and the National Lawyers Guild cited Tel Aviv’s ongoing genocide in Gaza and escalating settler violence in the occupied West Bank as absolute grounds to reject deeper integration.
A separate policy brief from A New Policy, co-founded by former State Department whistleblower Josh Paul, cautioned that embedding Israeli contractors exposes sensitive American capabilities to counterintelligence risks, disadvantages domestic firms, and systematically hides weapons transfers from public transparency.
While the House of Representatives text of the legislation appoints a Pentagon coordinator, the Senate version goes further by requiring direct, ongoing consultation with Israel’s war minister.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu celebrated the clause, boasting it converts his regime from a foreign aid recipient into a full-scale military partner.
A bipartisan amendment introduced by Representatives Thomas Massie (R) and Ro Khanna (D) to remove the provision was buried by House leadership.
With the current ten-year military aid agreement set to expire in 2028, Washington’s pro-Israel establishment is rushing to lock this structural merger into permanent law.
This legislative push comes as public backlash grows over the unprovoked U.S.-Israeli war against Iran and the Resistance Front.
If enacted, Section 219 will bind future administrations to Tel Aviv’s strategic interests regardless of voter demands.

articles.title: Air defense downs 128 of 167 Russian drones, impacts recorded at 23 locations
articles.body:
In the early hours of Saturday, the Defense Forces of Ukraine neutralized 128 Russian targets; however, impacts were recorded at 23 locations, according to the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
"According to preliminary data as of 08:30, air defense shot down/suppressed 128 Russian UAVs of the Shahed, Gerbera, and other types," the report states.
In total, overnight on September 5 (from 18:00 on September 4), Russia launched Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles from Rostov and Voronezh regions of Russia, as well as 167 strike UAVs of the Shahed type (about half of which were jet-powered), Gerbera, and decoy drones of Parodiya type from Orel, Millerovo, Kursk, temporarily occupied Donetsk, and Hvardiyske in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned system units, as well as mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.
Meanwhile, hits by Russian missiles and strike UAVs were recorded at 23 locations, with falling debris from downed targets recorded at one location. In addition, a portion of Russian strike assets failed to reach their targets, with further details currently being clarified.

articles.title: Who really benefits from the CIA chief’s Moscow trip?
articles.body:
Who really benefits from the CIA chief’s Moscow trip?
Speculation abounds over the reason for CIA Director John Ratcliffe’s recent trip to Moscow. Which probably could have been an email. Or a social media post. Just like everything else this administration does.
Oooh, don’t tell me! He went to demand that Russian President Vladimir Putin not help Iran! Or he went to ask whether they’re still up for more speed dating to talk peace in Ukraine! Or maybe just to talk about swapping prisoners. Which happens fairly regularly. And doesn’t require a personal visit. Or maybe Ratcliffe just had a jonesing for that ice cream at the GUM mall in Red Square. Who really knows.
So I’d like to personally take the opportunity to add to the theories, which can only really be evaluated sometime down the road in hindsight.
The thing that strikes me the most about this trip is the sudden secrecy. Specifically from an administration with a penchant for blabbing about everything. If Trump wanted to tell Putin or Russian intelligence something, he’d do it himself on Truth Social Instead, he was uncharacteristically vague, calling the trip semi-routine. When is this guy tight-lipped about anything? It’s so far out of character for the American President that one is almost obligated to look for a motive for the secrecy.
So with that in mind, it seems reasonable to ask whether there is any financial or political constituency that stands to benefit from the message being sent by this unusually secretive trip.
Well, it turns out that it just happened to take place at the same time as the European Union was meeting to set its new 7-year budget, and Eastern European Baltic nations were making a massive push for cash from Brussels.
You know what they say: if you have a pet that starts in with some nasty habits, like chewing the furniture to get your attention, then you really have to nip that in the bud real quick. Otherwise, there’s a risk that, next thing you know, your other pets will learn from it and start gnawing on the couch or the table legs, too.
So here you have Europe, that’s been sitting there while Kiev says 'gimme money', and 'I deserve it because I’m defending all of Europe for you. Oh, and even better, actually, defending DEMOCRACY for you lazy bums'. And instead of whacking it on the nose and going, 'NO, BAD! Brussels just goes, 'Wanna treat?'
So now, what do you know, here comes Latvia, who’s been watching this whole charade, seeing that Ukraine goes from begging to getting tossed a bone every single time, and now they too are like, 'Woof, woof, I’m defending all of Europe for you. Where’s my money? 7 BILLION EUROS, specifically'.
And it’s not like Latvia is even bothering to come up with its own twist on Ukraine’s pitch. It’s not like they’re saying, 'Ukraine’s pitch to Brussels is, ‘Look, we’re being invaded. You’d better give us what we want because we’re the only thing standing between Putin showing up in Europe with a neck pillow for an Interrail tour of Europe.’ So we, Latvia, need to come up with something else. Especially since we aren’t actually being invaded – we just need some emotional-support money'.
No, instead, they’re just basically saying the exact same sort of thing minus the existential threat – that Latvia is the bouncer at the Baltic door keeping Putin on the other side of the velvet rope.
Surely it can’t possibly have anything to do with the fact that Latvia’s economy could use the kind of economic boost that can only come from having Brussels dump a ton of cash into its defense industry, right? Because everything’s going so well for Latvia economically, ever since this conflict in Ukraine went hot in 2022 and Riga cut itself off from Russian trade: from just over €2 billion a year back then, to just €193 million last year – an almost 90% reduction in the value of trade between the two countries, according to Latvia’s own foreign affairs ministry.
And now energy prices are going back up again, too – an 83% spike in gas prices since the beginning of this year in Latvia, and 24% over just the past month. An established trend since the EU cut everyone off from Russian fuel and now Trump’s cutting everyone off from fuel from the Middle East with his apparently endless 'mine’s bigger' standoff with Iran.
Oh look, here comes Lithuania now, too. What a surprise! Another guy watching from the cheap seats and going: 'Hang on. We’re also next to Russia. We have security problems, infrastructure costs, and defense bills. Where is OUR cash handout?'
Turns out that Lithuania has just gone directly to Brussels with the invoice, essentially saying: You keep telling us the eastern flank is crucial to European security. Wonderful. Please prove this commitment using the traditional European unit of measurement: euros.
When it comes to Eastern Europe, the EU’s seven-year budget plan is starting to look like a group dinner where everyone suddenly remembers that the guy at the end of the table has a corporate credit card.
But the real question is whose bills would Brussels ultimately be paying? Surely it’s just a mere coincidence that major beneficiaries of Latvian and Lithuanian defense spending include Trump’s America, as the largest supplier of major conventional arms to Latvia and Lithuania, according to the most recently available Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI) arms transfer data.
All this comes after the western press reported that the CIA director flew to Moscow this week to tell Russia not to attack NATO countries. Which is actually great marketing for the cause of Eastern European countries shaking down Brussels and basically launching a grant program. They’re behaving now as though a potential future hypothetical Russian attack on NATO is serious enough to justify enormous new expenditures, but the benefit of Brussels’ largesse risks going to Washington as the top weapons supplier.
The trip is remarkably convenient for governments seeking to turn fears about Russia into a case for vastly increased European defense spending – and for the American defense industry that stands to benefit from a big chunk of that spending.
But hey, who really cares if everyone’s barking out for treats when you’re Brussels and all you ever need to do is reach into the pockets of the taxpayer. Even if you then run straight back to Uncle Sam with it and drop it in his lap.
The statements, views and opinions expressed in this column are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of RT.

articles.title: Israel’s Shin Bet has held Russian-Israeli historian Artem Kirpichenok for more than a month without disclosing why. His family says the case may involve espionage.
articles.body:
Israel’s Shin Bet has held Russian-Israeli historian Artem Kirpichenok for more than a month without disclosing why. His family says the case may involve espionage.
Historian and writer Artem Kirpichenok flew to Tel Aviv on August 2 to attend an international conference, his support group said. Officers from Israel’s General Security Service (Shin Bet) detained him at the airport. Kirpichenok, a citizen of both Russia and Israel, has remained in custody ever since. Officials have not disclosed the reason for his detention.
Little is known about Artem Kirpichenok’s case. Israeli authorities may suspect him of espionage.
Family representatives told Meduza that, based on “unofficial information,” investigators suspect Kirpichenok of espionage and of contacting an agent of a foreign intelligence service.
But “there’s no Arab angle [to the case],” the source said. According to the source, the agent Kirpichenok allegedly contacted is not from Lebanon or Iran.
“Who could it be, then? If it’s Russia, the whole case is built on sand, as Israelis say. He’s a Russian citizen who has lived in Russia permanently since 2005. And Russia is hardly a stranger to Israel: the two countries conduct joint intelligence operations and share information despite friction over Iran and other issues,” the source told Meduza.
The alleged offenses are considered serious, according to the source, but even Kirpichenok’s lawyer does not know exactly what he is accused of. Israeli law has more than a dozen statutes that can apply in espionage cases, with penalties of up to life imprisonment.
“The fact that someone is held in a Shin Bet detention facility indicates that the person is suspected of crimes against state security,” a representative of Kirpichenok’s family said.
A separate charge may stem from Kirpichenok’s 2018 trip to Iran, which he wrote about on social media at the time. Israel considers Iran an enemy state, and traveling there without special permission from the Israeli Interior Ministry carries a prison sentence of up to four years.
Nika Dubrovskaya, an artist and friend of Kirpichenok’s, told the outlet Bumaga that he visited Israel several times after his trip to Iran without running into problems at the border. Another friend of Kirpichenok’s told Meduza the account was accurate and said the historian had also visited Israel the previous winter, before his August trip.
He rented out his apartment in Ashkelon, which was one reason he returned to the country several times a year.
Kirpichenok’s research and columns
Kirpichenok, 51, holds a Doctor of Sciences degree and works as a journalist and researcher specializing in the Middle East and Central Asia. A family representative told Meduza that he is cautious — an “armchair scholar” who dislikes fieldwork.
A friend of Kirpichenok’s told Meduza that she met him in Israel in the mid-1990s, when she was living there and he was still studying at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. She said that after he graduated, Kirpichenok could not find work in his field in Israel and was “very unhappy.”
Kirpichenok, a St. Petersburg native, returned to Russia in the 2000s and inherited an apartment there, she said. During those years, he worked as a tour guide, gave lectures, and wrote articles: “He worked with all kinds of publications and held, I’d say, Trotskyist views. Some minor grassroots activity: tours, and during COVID, he developed routes like ‘Sick Petersburg.’ A kind of intellectual precariat.”
Drawing on his dissertation about Hungarian nationalist movements at the turn of the 20th century, Kirpichenok wrote a book titled Vengriya-1956: drugoy vzglyad (“Hungary-1956: A Different View”). Kirpichenok criticized the 1956 Hungarian uprising, viewing it not as a progressive movement against the Soviet regime but as a far-right conservative revolt.
In recent years, Kirpichenok headed the Slavic studies department at the Center for Arab-Eurasian Studies, which was founded by Amr Abdel-Hamid, an Egyptian journalist, media manager, and former head of Al Jazeera’s Moscow bureau.
He also wrote about the Middle East for the Turkish broadcaster TRT and the Azerbaijani outlet Caliber, sharply criticizing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s actions in Gaza, and its policies toward Palestinians.
In his book Izrail’. Put’ k katastrofe (“Israel: The Road to Catastrophe”), Kirpichenok says Israel is not “the revived state of the Jewish people” but “the last bastion of Western colonialism.”
“Artem never wrote anything that went beyond what he read in the newspaper Haaretz and a couple dozen other sources, like B’Tselem,” his friend said. “I mean, some criticism of the existing regime. Geez, that exists in every country, and it’s a good thing — that’s what the intelligentsia is for.”
She was surprised by the possibility of espionage charges: “He doesn’t have any [classified] information. How would he have access to any?”
Kirpichenok flew to Israel for an academic conference — but officials in the city where it was supposed to take place had never heard of it
Kirpichenok is now being held in a Shin Bet pretrial detention facility in Petah Tikva.
He is alone in a cell where the lights stay on around the clock, with no outdoor exercise and no access to reading or writing materials. “All he can do in his cell is sit or lie down, sleep, or think,” a family representative said.
“Before October 7, 2023, only Arab Muslims were subjected to this kind of repression,” a representative of Kirpichenok’s family told Meduza.
A support group of Kirpichenok’s friends believes the international conference may have been a trap set by security services to get the scholar into the country, according to the independent Russian outlet Doxa. Kirpichenok arrived in Israel on August 2 and had planned to leave six days later.
Representatives of Kirpichenok’s family contacted the municipality of the city where the conference was supposedly scheduled to take place, but officials there said no such event had been held. The family said Kirpichenok avoided answering questions about exactly who had invited him to Israel.
Israeli security officers pressured Kirpichenok, according to a family representative
The fourth court hearing in Kirpichenok’s case took place in Ashkelon on Thursday, August 27. The proceedings are closed to the public.
Kirpichenok was brought to court from the pretrial detention facility. Family representatives said he was held in a soundproof glass booth during the hearing. His lawyer, Inna Lebedinskaya-Katz, was unable to speak with her client during the proceedings, a Meduza source said. (Lebedinskaya-Katz declined to comment, citing a court order barring publication of details about Kirpichenok’s case.)
That day, the court extended the gag order on details of Kirpichenok’s case through August 31. A formal declaration of charges — roughly equivalent to an indictment in Russian legal procedure — was due to be filed on September 4. At that point, the defense would be able to access the investigation files, a family representative told Meduza. The family representative expects prosecutors to seek Kirpichenok’s continued detention through the end of the trial.
At the hearing, Lebedinskaya-Katz asked the court to exclude her client’s confession, arguing that Kirpichenok had been pressured into making it. Israel Shamir, a left-wing Israeli writer and columnist covering the case, said on Telegram that Lebedinskaya-Katz had filed the motion.
Kirpichenok had not been allowed to contact his lawyer, a family representative told Meduza. His only meeting with his defense attorney came on August 23, when he told Lebedinskaya-Katz that he had falsely incriminated himself “under pressure from investigators.”
During that meeting, Kirpichenok, in handcuffs, was held in a glass booth and spoke with his lawyer by phone. He feared the conversation might be monitored and worried that he would “be sent back down to the basement” where the interrogations took place, a family representative told Meduza.
Investigators allegedly threatened to confiscate his apartment in Israel and deport him to Ukraine. “He never supported the ‘special military operation’ that Russia launched, but because he holds left-wing views, he has spoken out against imperialism, including Russian imperialism,” a family representative told Meduza. There is no independent confirmation that investigators pressured Kirpichenok.
At the August 27 hearing, Kirpichenok “looked much worse” than he had when he met with his lawyer. According to Shamir, the defense attorney said: “His face seemed to sag, his eyes were dull, and he could barely smile.”
Lebedinskaya-Katz asked the court to move Kirpichenok from pretrial detention to house arrest because he has an apartment in Ashkelon, but the judge denied the request, citing the severity of the charges.
Kirpichenok also asked for an interpreter at future hearings — a request that surprised representatives of his family, since he had begun living in Israel as a teenager, served in the Israel Defense Forces, and later graduated from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
The lawyer asked the court to allow a psychiatrist to see her client, citing his depressed state and post-traumatic stress disorder.
How Russia reacted to Kirpichenok’s detention
“The irony of Artem’s situation is that he holds two toxic passports. Neither country is particularly eager to stand up for him, you know?” the historian’s friend told Meduza.
Kirpichenok’s support group only recently contacted Russia’s Foreign Ministry, and Russian diplomats “have been emphatic in promising their support,” a family representative told Meduza. But because Kirpichenok also holds Israeli citizenship, Russian Embassy staff have not yet been allowed to see him.
Russia’s ambassador to Israel, Anatoly Viktorov, said the diplomatic mission “had sent a request to the appropriate Israeli authorities.”
Valery Fadeev, head of the Presidential Human Rights Council, sent a letter to Matthew Gillett, chair-rapporteur of the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, on August 28. In the letter, Fadeev said: “In Israel, this kind of detention is usually linked to suspected crimes against state security.”
“This suggests that his detention was motivated by [Kirpichenok’s] political views,” the letter says. “Of particular concern is his health: he suffers from hypertension with a risk of retinal detachment, which requires constant medical monitoring.”
The Presidential Human Rights Council called on the United Nations to demand that Israeli authorities clarify the grounds for Kirpichenok’s detention and ensure that he has immediate access to a lawyer and qualified medical care.
Shin Bet had not responded to Meduza’s request for comment as of publication.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].

articles.title: Analysis: Pro-Russia AfD Eyes First German State Government as Support Surges
articles.body:
Germany enters a decisive month of state elections with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) closer to executive power than at any point in its history.
Saxony-Anhalt votes on Sunday, Sept. 6. The latest projection gives the AfD 41%, almost twice the 20.8% it received in the previous state election in 2021. The governing Christian Democratic Union (CDU) trails on 23%.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
In practical terms, approximately two out of every five voters now support the AfD, while only slightly more than one in five backs the CDU. The AfD could become the largest party by an 18-point margin, although the projection indicates that an outright parliamentary majority remains unlikely.
The party is also leading in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, which votes on Sept. 20. An Infratest dimap poll puts the AfD at 35%, narrowly ahead of the governing Social Democratic Party (SPD) with 32%.
The AfD received 16.7% there in 2021. It has therefore more than doubled its support in the last five years, while the SPD has fallen from 39.6%.
Berlin votes on the same day. The AfD is not leading there, but its support has risen to approximately 18%, compared with 9.1% in the city’s 2023 repeat election.
From eastern protest party to national force
The September elections form part of a longer rise.
The AfD received 10.4% in Germany’s 2021 federal election. Four years later, it doubled that result to 20.8%, becoming the country’s second-largest party in the Bundestag. National polling now places it at approximately 28%, ahead of Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU/CSU bloc.
Kyiv Airports Struck in Response to US Diplomacy, Zelensky Says
The party remains strongest in the formerly communist east, but its growth is no longer confined there.
“The AfD has much greater popularity in the eastern, so-called new federal states than in the old ones,” Berlin-based journalist Nikolai Klimeniouk told Kyiv Post.
“But its popularity is also growing sharply in western Germany.” Klimeniouk linked the trend to a broader loss of trust in mainstream politics.
“There is a sense of a general crisis of democracy and distrust toward it,” he said. “It is understandable that anti-liberal populist forces gain support under such conditions.”
The same trajectory was identified after the AfD’s strong results in Saxony and Thuringia in 2024.
Foreign-policy expert Benjamin Tallis said that voters were concerned about Germany’s decline and the absence of a credible future. Many believed they were not being heard on inflation and migration – issues to which the governing parties had failed to provide convincing answers.
Tallis warned that populist parties would continue rising unless Germany’s democratic parties “get their act together.”
That prediction has been confirmed. However, Tallis also cautioned against interpreting every AfD vote as a direct rejection of support for Ukraine.
State elections do not determine foreign policy, and Ukraine was not among the principal concerns reported by AfD voters in 2024.
No weapons for Ukraine, no sanctions on Russia
The AfD’s federal program calls for an end to German weapons deliveries to Ukraine, the removal of sanctions against Russia, and negotiations that would leave Ukraine outside both NATO and the EU.
Its official foreign-policy platform states: “The USA remains our partner. Russia should become one.”
The party supports restoring economic relations with Moscow and reopening the Nord Stream pipelines.
That would revive the energy model that former Ukrainian Ambassador to Germany Andriy Melnyk described to Kyiv Post as Germany’s “self-inflicted Russian dependency.”
Germany began breaking with that model following Russia’s full-scale invasion, including by reducing its reliance on Russian energy and supplying increasingly advanced weapons to Ukraine, a change Kyiv Post documented in 2022.
The AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt parliamentary group has opposed Ukraine’s accession to NATO and the EU, rejected weapons deliveries, and backed continued use of Nord Stream 2.
The state party’s 2026 program goes even further, proposing that Ukrainians in Germany no longer be recognized as war refugees. It argues that Ukrainians affected by fighting should seek protection in western Ukraine instead.
AfD leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla boycotted President Volodymyr Zelensky’s 2024 Bundestag address. They called him a “war and beggar president,” questioned his legitimacy, and accused him of seeking German money for reconstruction.
The Russian sympathies became particularly visible following the attempted explosive-drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4.
The German government concluded that people acting for Russian state agencies were responsible. Berlin responded by closing Russia’s consulate general in Bonn and terminating the agreement governing the Russian House cultural center in Berlin.
As Kyiv Post reported, the Russian House is operated by the sanctioned Kremlin agency Rossotrudnichestvo and has faced accusations of spreading propaganda, supporting Russian influence operations and pressuring journalists through litigation.
Despite Berlin’s announcement, the center can remain open until its governing agreement expires in June 2027.
However, Chrupalla accused the government of applying “double standards.” He said he would have welcomed an equivalent response to what he described as Ukraine’s attack on the Nord Stream pipelines.
Meanwhile, the AfD’s Saxony-Anhalt program calls for closer economic and cultural relations with Russia and expanded Russian-language teaching in schools. It describes the established parties’ “anti-Russian policy” as contrary to German interests.
What an AfD state government could actually do.
Winning a state election would not give the AfD control over German foreign policy.
Under Germany’s Basic Law, relations with foreign states are conducted by the federal government. Foreign affairs and defense fall under exclusive federal jurisdiction.
An AfD minister-president in Magdeburg or Schwerin could not end German weapons deliveries to Ukraine, lift EU sanctions, reopen Nord Stream, or withdraw Germany from NATO.
A state government would nevertheless control institutions with substantial power over everyday life.
Germany’s states are responsible for education, culture, and most policing. An AfD government could reshape school curricula, redirect cultural funding, alter integration programs, appoint senior civil servants, and place its own ministers above the state police and domestic intelligence service.
That last possibility has created particular concern in Saxony-Anhalt, where the state intelligence service has classified the AfD branch as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization.
An AfD interior minister could oversee the same state agency that monitors the party. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has already said classified information should not be shared with AfD officials if the party enters government, citing its proximity to Vladimir Putin.
A state government would also represent Saxony-Anhalt in the Bundesrat, the chamber through which Germany’s states participate in federal legislation. One state could not overturn Berlin’s policy alone, but it could use its votes, ministries, and political platform to obstruct legislation and promote closer relations with Moscow.
The larger risk for Ukraine
All major German parties continue to rule out forming coalitions with the AfD. Winning the most votes would therefore not automatically make AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund state premier.
But an AfD result above 40% could leave the other parties unable to form a stable majority without alliances they have also rejected. That could produce a fragile minority government or increase pressure on the CDU to reconsider its firewall against cooperation with the far right.
For Ukraine, the immediate danger is not that Saxony-Anhalt will suddenly take control of German foreign policy. It’s the possibility of the AfD gaining its first record of executive government, normalizing its pro-Russia program, and forcing every other party to respond to its success before the next federal election in 2029.
In 2024, Tallis warned that mainstream politicians could misread regional protest votes as demands to reduce support for Ukraine. Two years later, the AfD is substantially stronger, its position toward Kyiv is unchanged, and the party is closer than ever to acquiring real state power.

articles.title: Putin shows ‘saint-like patience’ – former US judge (VIDEO)

Putin shows ‘saint-like patience’ – former US judge (VIDEO)
Russia has the right to strike NATO plants making weapons for Ukraine, but President Vladimir Putin is showing great restraint to avoid a direct clash with the bloc, former American judge Andrew Napolitano has said.
Kiev has been launching hundreds of fixed-wing drones deep into Russian territory on a daily basis in recent months, many of which are manufactured in European countries. Earlier this year, the Defense Ministry in Moscow published a list of enterprises producing the UAVs, some of which are based in the UK, Germany, Italy, Czechia, and other NATO-member states. London and Paris are currently also discussing plans to make long-range SCALP/Storm Shadow missiles in Ukraine.
In an interview with RT on Friday, Napolitano, who hosts the popular ‘Judging Freedom’ interview channel on YouTube, said that “President Putin has demonstrated an almost saint-like capacity for patience and forbearance” by not ordering Russian forces to target those facilities.
“Under international law, he would have every right to strike at the munitions plants and the military, not the civilians… of the countries that are producing the weapons that are striking deep into Russia,” he said.
“I’m sure he understands that. My guess is that he’s considered it, but he’s been consistently patient. Sometimes even to the dismay of his strongest supporters,” the former New Jersey Superior Court judge added.
Putin is focused on the Ukraine conflict and “does not want a war against NATO,” he argued.
The Russian president previously labeled claims of Moscow having aggressive designs against the bloc as “nonsense,” saying that they are only made by Western politicians to distract the public from problems at home and justify growing military spending.
However, Moscow warned the UK in late August that its military facilities and equipment in Ukraine and beyond could become legitimate targets for Russia if Kiev continues to use British-supplied weapons for strikes on Russian territory.
Russian officials also said that if Latvia, Estonia, and Lithuania knowingly helped to facilitate Ukrainian drone attacks against northwestern Russia, Moscow could consider them complicit in those actions and would have the right to self-defense under the UN Charter.
Napolitano said that the Ukraine conflict is “headed into an acceleration” and that he expects “a last-ditched effort by some of the NATO countries to try and prevent the inevitable, which is the achievement by the Russian military of its objectives.”
“The Ukrainians are aware that they’re on their last legs, so to speak, in the war. They know that their days are numbered,” he stressed.

“Clearly, these Russian strikes on the airports are a reaction to the discussions and preparations for the possibility of the U.S. side using an aircraft to travel to Ukraine and land at Kyiv Airport or Boryspil Airport,” Zelenskyy wrote on US social media company X.

“Russian-Iranian ‘shaheds’ in response to American diplomacy,” he said. “We have taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky.”
Zelenskyy said Kyiv would not allow threats to undermine diplomacy from its side, stressing that Ukraine is interested in bringing peace closer.
“Russia will be held accountable for what it does,” he said.
Axios and Russian state news agency Tass reported, citing sources, that the two US envoys would visit Moscow and Kyiv over the weekend.
Zelenskyy said Witkoff and Kushner would visit Kyiv on Sunday after their trip to Moscow.
The two envoys have never visited Kyiv, while both have made several trips to Moscow since US-mediated talks began.

"Russian-Iranian Shaheds in response to American diplomacy," Zelensky said, adding that Kyiv would adjust its operations regarding Russian airspace next week in response to the strikes.

articles.title: Iranian leadership considers escalation as US officials fear military, cyberattacks - report
articles.body:
Iran may be considering a significant escalation in its war with the United States, having grown more confident in its ability to attack targets in the Middle East, The New York Times reported on Friday, citing recent US intelligence reports.
Throughout the war, Iran gained a better understanding of its military strengths and confidence regarding its capabilities, leading to a reluctance among Iranian leaders to make any sort of agreement to fully end the war, according to the report.
In recent weeks, Iran has resumed strikes against US targets in the Middle East and the US has resumed strikes within Iran, but US officials fear that Iran may intensify their attacks both within the Middle East, targeting more ships in the Strait of Hormuz and US infrastructure in the region and within the cybersphere, mounting cyberattacks on essential US domestic systems, the NYT wrote.
Cyberattacks believed to have been perpetrated by Iran-linked hackers
According to the report, US officials believe Iran-linked hackers were behind cyberattacks on more than 100 water systems across the US in July.
While no systems were degraded to the point of making water unsafe to drink, the attacks caused disruptions that required manual overrides and precautionary boil-water advisories.
US oil and gas infrastructure may also be on the hackers' target list, current and former US officials told the NYT, although those systems are more protected.
It is unclear whether any energy systems have been breached, the NYT wrote.
In addition to any actual disruptions to US systems, former intelligence officials and security experts told the NYT that Iran may use the opportunity to increase the unpopularity of the war.
“Even if such attacks fail to meaningfully unsettle the American public, they can still play into a broader effort to exhaust domestic patience with this administration’s handling of the conflict,” Alex Orleans, a former US government cybersecurity contractor who specializes in tracking Iranian hacking groups, told the NYT.
Iran has also gained a more precise understanding of its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, and believes that US forces will not be able to sustain major new strikes due to dwindling munition stockpiles, according to the report.
Iran focuses on US elections
Additionally, knowing the war is unpopular, in part due to high gas prices, Iranian leaders may want to drag the war out until at least the midterms.
“The Iranians think they have maximum leverage,” the NYT cited Representative Josh Gottheimer, Democrat of New Jersey, as saying. “So, from their perspective, why not keep sticking it to the president?”
Signs of Iran spreading propaganda against Trump have emerged, with Meta releasing a report highlighting a network of Facebook and Instagram accounts originating in Iran and focused on US politics, including "anti-Republican views."
Domestic media in Iran has also published more than 1,200 Persian-language articles within the past two weeks about Trump and the midterm elections, according to threat intelligence company Alethea.
While the Trump administration has focused on economic sanctions, one member of the Intelligence Committee told the NYT he expected Iran to endure the measures.
“Because the Iranian government does not care much about the suffering of its people, it has been able to withstand both punishing economic sanctions and military bombardments,” he was cited as saying.

It is noted that, in many respects, these assessments reflect what is being observed on the ground, where hostilities have flared up again after a period of relative calm. Over the past week, Iran has attacked vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and U.S. forces in the region, while U.S. armed forces have carried out strikes on Iranian territory, resulting in the deaths of military personnel and civilians.
For now, the new clashes remain limited in scope. However, according to people who have reviewed the reports, they indicate that "Iran's hard-line government may be considering the possibility of a significant escalation of the conflict."

Some current and former officials said the reports indicate that reaching any agreement on a complete end to the war will be difficult. According to some officials, "little indicates that Iran is ready to reach any deal with the United States, contenting itself with deepening President Trump's political problems ahead of the U.S. midterm elections."
At present, Trump is not seeking negotiations and has said that, in his view, he can apply economic pressure on Iran that will force Tehran to make concessions regarding control of the strait and, possibly, ultimately, its nuclear program. However, according to officials who have reviewed the intelligence reports, in the short term, U.S. economic sanctions are likely to continue provoking an escalation of the conflict.
"In the coming weeks, Iran may take actions similar to those it took in July. At that time, Iran attacked U.S. military bases in the Middle East, killing three Americans in Jordan; struck shipping in the Strait of Hormuz; and also attacked infrastructure in Kuwait and elsewhere," the publication's sources said.

articles.title: The US called on Ukraine and russia to suspend strikes during Witkoff’s and Kushner’s visits to moscow and Kyiv — media reports
articles.body:
The US called on Ukraine and russia to suspend strikes during Witkoff’s and Kushner’s visits to moscow and Kyiv — media reports
Kyiv • UNN
Witkoff and Kushner will visit moscow and Kyiv to resume peace talks. The US called on the parties to temporarily halt strikes.
The United States is insisting that the Ukrainians temporarily halt their drone attacks on moscow and the country's energy facilities, and that the Russians halt their missile attacks on Kyiv during the visit of U.S. President's special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to the capitals of the russian federation and Ukraine, UNN reports, citing the NYT.
Details
Two of U.S. President Donald Trump's top emissaries, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, are heading to moscow and Kyiv this weekend to resume negotiations on a peace deal that would end the four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine, officials familiar with the diplomatic efforts said.
Witkoff, the American leader's special envoy, and Kushner, his son-in-law and frequent key negotiator, are expected to meet with Russian President vladimir putin on Saturday. They will then travel to Kyiv for the first time to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
According to officials, talks over the trip have been underway for weeks, with the United States insisting that the Ukrainians temporarily halt their drone attacks on moscow and the country's energy facilities while the two men are in russia, and that the Russians similarly halt their missile attacks on Kyiv. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a trip that has not been officially announced.
The publication notes that it is unclear whether the Americans are offering both presidents new proposals or pushing them to narrow the gap on the remaining issues, including who will ultimately control the Donbas, Ukrainian territory partially occupied by russia.
Although Witkoff and Kushner have traveled to moscow several times, they have not been to Kyiv, despite numerous official invitations. Two weeks ago, CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited moscow, where he stayed for only a few hours to meet with his Russian counterpart. Witkoff has seen putin more than half a dozen times.
The meeting is taking place at a dangerous moment in the conflict. For much of the year, Ukraine's attacks on oil refineries and other energy targets have had a devastating impact, forcing Russians to stand in line for hours to get gasoline, if they can find it at all. But the Ukrainians have run out of interceptor missiles to stop Russian missiles raining down on Ukraine, leaving Kyiv and some other cities almost defenseless.
President Trump has sought to bring russia back into the fold: he and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent invited russia to take part in the Group of 20 finance ministers' meeting last week in North Carolina, despite objections from European allies. russia has been excluded from many diplomatic meetings since its invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
To remind
Zelenskyy stated that U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would visit moscow on Saturday and that Ukraine guarantees the "normal functioning of Russian airspace," while they are expected in Kyiv on Sunday.
Context
Back in July, it was reported that U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner agreed to visit Kyiv for the first time as part of peace efforts to end the war.
At the end of August, it was reported that Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Ukraine, amid intensified russian missile and drone attacks on Kyiv, had been postponed but not canceled.
On September 3, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that a visit by U.S. President's special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Kyiv could take place in the coming days, but that they would first visit moscow.
On September 3, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced "new momentum" in peace efforts to end russia's war against Ukraine, with the return of an active political and diplomatic phase, but noted that achieving this without the participation of the American side was unrealistic.
On September 4, a source in the Russian media reported that American negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner would visit Russia and Ukraine on Saturday and Sunday, September 5 and 6.

articles.title: Scott Bessent met with Russia’s finance minister. Then he said Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy sites were helping fuel a global ‘energy shock.’
articles.body:
Scott Bessent met with Russia’s finance minister. Then he said Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy sites were helping fuel a global ‘energy shock.’
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure one of the causes of the global energy crisis. He spoke after a meeting of G20 finance ministers in North Carolina, to which Anton Siluanov, Russia’s finance minister, was invited for the first time since the start of the war.
“Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets and refined products,” Bessent said on Fox News, adding that the attacks were contributing to an energy shock and putting upward pressure on prices globally. He also cited the U.S. war with Iran, but stressed that the conflict would come to an end.
Siluanov’s presence at the summit — and his bilateral talks with Bessent — drew criticism from Ukraine’s allies. Anton Gerashchenko, a former adviser to Ukraine’s interior minister, pushed back on Bessent’s remarks, arguing that his framing transforms Ukraine “from a victim of Russian aggression into a cause of a global problem” and “reverses cause and effect.” The energy crisis, he said, is driven primarily by wars, and the U.S.–Iran conflict has had a far greater impact on global markets.
Gerashchenko stressed that the United States wants to cut Russia’s energy revenues without reducing Russian energy supplies to global markets, and that rising gas prices ahead of November’s midterm elections have forced the Trump administration to find a “convenient explanation.”
Those elections and fears of another spike in fuel prices have already slowed passage of a new sanctions bill targeting Russia in the House of Representatives, Bloomberg reported.
The bill was drafted by the late Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina. It would allow the United States to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on imports from countries that are among the largest buyers of Russian oil and gas — chiefly China, India, and Turkey. The Senate passed it by an overwhelming majority in August, but the House has been less receptive, with lawmakers concerned that removing Russian oil from the global market could push gas prices even higher amid the war with Iran.
Ukraine is trying to persuade Congress not to delay the sanctions. Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the Ukrainian president’s commissioner for sanctions policy, traveled to Washington this week to meet with members of Congress and said Ukraine was “quite optimistic” about the level of support for the bill. “Everyone agreed that it was necessary to increase pressure on Russia,” Vlasiuk said. “No one said that he definitely would not support this bill.”
The European Union, meanwhile, is weighing new restrictions on Russia. After Germany blamed Moscow for a failed drone attack at Leipzig Airport, European diplomats plan to discuss curbing tourist visas for Russians, restricting Russian diplomats’ travel within the EU, and sanctioning additional vessels in Russia’s “shadow fleet,” Bloomberg reported.
The war in photos: Brovary, Kyiv region
Industrial sites in the Brovary district of the Kyiv region have been burning for a second straight day after Russian strikes. A drone hit a Coca-Cola plant on September 3, and warehouses caught fire after another strike on the morning of September 4.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis launch first major offensive in four years
articles.body:
