articles.title: Guard F-16s Kept Pace on Kadena Deployment, but Edge Wears Thin
articles.body:
An F-16 Air National Guard unit’s six-month deployment to Kadena Air Base, Japan, this year illustrated the capabilities the Guard’s oldest fighter units can still offer—but also the challenges they face, officials told reporters this week.
On one hand, leaders said the Colorado ANG’s 120th Fighter Squadron was largely able to keep pace with its fifth-generation teammates and hone its Agile Combat Employment skills throughout the Pacific.
But on the other, the squadron’s 1980s-era F-16s are starting to show their age and lack at least some of the high-end capabilities the Air Force has said it wants to prioritize for a high-end fight.
“We’re able to keep up, with the exception of obviously being a fourth‑gen airplane,” Lt. Col. Frank “Chester” Prokop, squadron commander and detachment commander during the deployment, said. “We can’t get nearly as close to surface‑to‑air threats or air‑to‑air threats posed by China over there as some of the newer models. So, we’re kind of getting to the end of our capability. We’ve maxed it out. We played the perfect game.”
The January-to-June deployment, part of a rotation of fighters through Kadena as the base waits for its new F-15EX Eagle IIs, is a signpost of things to come for both the Air Force’s total fighter fleet, but more specifically for challenges faced inside the Air National Guard. The fleet is getting older while replacements are slowly ordered and delivered, and with the Active-Duty force being prioritized, the Guard is pushing the envelope with its legacy aircraft.
“The first piece is that any aging airframe is going to negatively impact operational availability and daily ops tempo,” Heather Penney, a former F-16 fighter pilot who now serves as the director of studies and research at the Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies. “I mean, you could talk about taking your 35‑year‑old car to an F1 race. Is that really what you want to do?”
Six Months at Kadena
Originally, the 120th was supposed to deploy a dozen of its F-16C Block 30 jets to Kadena from January to May. But that stay was extended six weeks due to demands across the Air Force related to Operation Epic Fury and the conflict with Iran. The conflict also impacted plans to join exercises in Thailand.
Still, the Guardsmen and their jets got to put into practice the Agile Combat Employment training they—with the rest of the Air Force—have been putting in for years now. ACE envisions small teams of Airmen dispersing from large central hubs to operate from remote or austere airfields, and the 120th implemented that through “small-package movements,” shuffling two to six jets around the region.
Prokop and 140th Wing Command Col. Christopher “KojaCk” Melka said the unit can now generate detailed ACE deployment packages, including personnel, aircraft load, and ground equipment needs, in 10-15 minutes, rather than the weeklong planning cycles common only a few years ago.
For a Philippines deployment, the squadron took four F-16s with a C-130 and worked with Marine Corps units. For Exercise Beverly Midnight at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, Japan, the unit conducted hot-pit refueling and rearming work alongside F-35s.
The unit also employed the “Multi-Capable Airman” approach to shrink its maintenance manpower footprint, Melka said. Operating mostly out of Kadena, a smaller package of cross-trained airmen handled various maintenance tasks for the squadron, rather than relying on a larger footprint with specialized technicians.
“We’ve actually exposed some of our Airmen to other career fields to give them a little bit more background on both, so that if, for whatever reason, they found themselves in a more austere environment where we could only send a certain package of maintainers and support personnel, maybe one person covered the duties of two,” Melka said.
Recap Ripple Effects
While the 120th was able to practice concepts like Agile Combat Employment and Multi-Capable Airmen during its deployment, the unit also had to stretch to keep its F-16s going, Melka and Prokop said.
“When these F-16s were first produced, it was roughly about six to eight maintenance man-hours per flight hour,” Prokop said. “Now, our maintainers are averaging 15 to 20 maintenance man-hours for every hour of flight.”
That’s because issues that require more in-depth maintenance, such as structural failures such as cracks on the airframe, “are happening at a much increasing rate right now,” Prokop said. “And that is probably the biggest challenge that we face is our maintenance unit has not received any increase in manpower commensurate with the level of increased requirements for maintenance time on the aircraft.”
The unit has been fortunate, the lieutenant colonel said, to have experienced, veteran maintainers working those airframes. But the increased maintenance needs are pushing leadership to make adjustments, like using more simulator flight time rather than flying hours to keep pilots sharp.
“The capacity of our maintainers to keep them safe and keep them combat effective is still working very well,” Melka said.
The jets themselves have also been upgraded many times over the years to stay effective with things like new AESA radars, Link 16 data links, and ongoing software upgrades; Prokop noted the F-16 has an unofficial nickname of the “Burger King jet” as a reference to the fast-food chain’s “Have It Your Way” slogan.
Nevertheless, the decades-old aircraft, while competent now, are closer to the end of their service lives—and the 120th is one of around a dozen Guard squadrons that have not been officially selected to recapitalize their fleets with newer aircraft such as the F-35A or F-15EX, leaving the unit’s future in doubt.
For now, Penney said, units like the 120th can keep flying their F-16s. But the Air Force has yet to signal its long-term plan for them and currently isn’t buying new jets fast enough to replace the older jets anytime soon.
“The Air Force has got to recapitalize at a meaningful rate, because they have deferred and delayed increasing their recapitalization rate,” Penney said. “If you want to be recapitalized by 2035, you’ve got to buy more than 100 fighters a year.”
Service leaders have said they need to procure at least 72 fighters per year to keep the fleet’s age from increasing. But the last time the service managed to budget for that was in fiscal 2024.
In fiscal 2025, the budget request was for 60 fighters. In 2026, it dropped to a low of 45. The fiscal 2027 request, still pending, is for just 62 fighters.
And even then, these new fighters—the F-35 and F-15EX—are mostly going to the Active-Duty force, leaving the Guard to wait. That could have a ripple effect, as the Guard deploys in nearly any major contingency or large-scale operation as a need, not an add-on, Penney said.
“If the Air Force does not recapitalize the Guard in a concurrent and proportional manner, they risk not only losing a key element of the total force, but they risk leaving the Guard with operationally irrelevant airframes,” Penney said.

articles.title: Russia’s elite drone unit says it used 1 million FPV drones
articles.body:
- Russia's Rubicon drone unit claims it used over 1 million FPV drones and struck 280,000 targets in Ukraine from January 2025 to August 2026, an unverified, self-reported figure.
- Independent analysts say Rubicon grew from 1,450 to about 5,000 personnel by 2026, but that Ukraine has since regained an edge in mid-range drone warfare.
Russia’s Rubicon Center for Advanced Unmanned Technologies claims its operators used more than 1 million First-Person-View (FPV) drones and struck over 280,000 targets in Ukraine between January 2025 and August 2026, according to a statement the unit posted to its official Telegram channel. The figures come only from Russia’s elite drone unit itself and have not been independently verified.
Rubicon said the 20-month total makes it “the undisputed leader” in FPV drone use among all Russian units fighting in Ukraine. The unit also said it has published more than 45,000 videos of strikes on its Telegram channel, with new footage posted daily showing operations, tactics and the unit’s history.
As with the strike and drone-use figures, these numbers are self-reported by the unit and cannot be independently confirmed.
Rubicon was established on August 2, 2024, by order of Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov, according to reporting by the newsletter Two Marines, run by analyst Rob Lee and Ukrainian marine drone operator Dmytro Putiata. The center was created partly in response to Ukraine’s own specialized drone units and its “Drone Line” initiative, and was designed to centralize Russian research, procurement and combat deployment of drones, ground robots and unmanned boats under one command, rather than leaving that work scattered across volunteer-funded projects.
An investigation by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty identified the unit’s commander as Colonel Sergei Budnikov, a 37-year-old former artillery and marine officer, with facilities including a training site at Patriot Park near Moscow.
Independent reporting has documented Rubicon’s rapid growth. The unit expanded from roughly 1,450 personnel in 2025 to about 5,000 by 2026, organized into battalion-sized detachments that each field dozens of quadcopter and fixed-wing strike teams, according to the Foreign Policy Research Institute’s analysis of the Two Marines data. That same analysis cautioned that Rubicon’s fast expansion has strained its recruitment pipeline and diluted the specialized training that made its early detachments effective.
Rubicon first drew significant attention for its role helping Russian forces cut off Ukrainian supply lines during the fighting in Russia’s Kursk Oblast in late 2024 and early 2025, after Ukraine’s surprise incursion there in August 2024. Ukrainian commanders quoted in independent reporting described the unit’s fiber-optic guided drones, which resist electronic jamming, as a serious problem, and Rubicon has continued operating on active fronts including the Kupiansk axis, where a Ukrainian brigade officer told Ukrainian outlet Suspilne in October that the unit’s use of remote mining and FPV drones was disrupting Ukrainian logistics.
Independent assessments diverge from Rubicon’s own self-promotion, however. While the unit’s tactics contributed to Russian gains around Pokrovsk, Myrnohrad and Kostyantynivka in 2025, the Foreign Policy Research Institute’s analysis found that Rubicon did not fundamentally change the broader stalemate in drone warfare along the front, and that by 2026 Ukraine had regained an edge in mid-range drone operations. Neither Rubicon’s claimed strike totals nor its claim of “undisputed” leadership among Russian drone units have been corroborated by Ukrainian officials or independent battlefield analysts.

articles.title: Yemeni gov't launches airstrikes on Houthi positions near Bab al-Mandab Strait: official
articles.body:
ADEN, Yemen, Sept. 4 (Xinhua) -- Yemeni government warplanes struck Houthi-held areas in the western provinces of Hodeidah and Taiz on Friday, backing ground troops battling a major Houthi offensive near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, a military official told Xinhua.
The airstrikes came as fierce fighting raged across multiple fronts in the two provinces, where Houthi fighters had made rapid advances over the past 24 hours, the official said on condition of anonymity.
The official said the warplanes targeted Houthi positions and movements in areas of active ground combat. Further details on the strikes or casualties were not immediately available.
A Houthi military source confirmed the strikes but attributed them to "Saudi aggression warplanes." Saudi Arabia has yet to comment.
As fighting intensified, Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), vowed on Friday that government forces would block the Houthis from advancing toward the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a vital waterway linking the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
The latest escalation, which erupted at dawn Thursday, has since claimed at least 90 lives, including 40 government soldiers and at least 50 Houthi fighters, across the two provinces, according to medical officials.
Yemen has been embroiled in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen. A Saudi-led coalition intervened the following year in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. ■

articles.title: New images show China’s largest stealth drone in testing
articles.body:
- New satellite images show China's largest known stealth drone, unofficially called the WZ-X, undergoing testing at Malan Air Base in Xinjiang.
- Analysts estimate its wingspan at about 52 meters, wider than a B-2 bomber, with a range exceeding 20,000 kilometers, though China has not confirmed the aircraft's existence.
New satellite images have surfaced showing China’s largest known stealth drone undergoing testing at a secretive air base in China’s Xinjiang region, according to analysts tracking the program on social media.
Aviation researcher Andreas Rupprecht posted on LinkedIn that two new images had leaked showing the aircraft, known unofficially as the WZ-X, at what appears to be Malan Air Base. A separate image cited by defense outlet The War Zone and shared on social media showed the aircraft’s trailing edge in detail, describing it as “shallowly serrated,” a shaping technique used to reduce a stealth aircraft’s radar signature.
Neither China’s government nor its military has confirmed the aircraft’s existence, name or purpose. Everything known about the WZ-X comes from commercial satellite imagery and the analysts who study it.
Malan Air Base, located in the Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, has become the Chinese air force’s primary test site for uncrewed aircraft, according to Rupprecht, who has researched Chinese military aviation and aircraft serial numbers for years. The base also hosts the 178th UAV Brigade. Satellite imagery dating back to 2022 shows the site expanding steadily, with new hangars and taxiways that analysts believe are tied to the WZ-X and a second, still-unidentified stealth combat drone known as the GJ-X. Rupprecht compared Malan to Area 51 in the United States, both for its remote desert location and for its role housing China’s most secretive aircraft programs.
The WZ-X was first identified in satellite imagery in 2024, with additional images captured through 2025 and 2026. Analysts describe it as a twin-engine flying-wing design, similar in overall layout to the U.S. Air Force’s classified RQ-180 drone but considerably larger. Estimates place its wingspan at roughly 52 meters (173 feet), wider than a B-2 Spirit bomber, with a length of about 14 meters (46 feet).
The War Zone has reported that its wingspan makes it the largest Chinese flying-wing design identified to date.
Rupprecht said the aircraft’s two engines appear to draw air through a single intake mounted on top of the fuselage, reportedly shielded with a conformal mesh intended to reduce the aircraft’s radar cross-section. Analysts estimate the drone’s range at more than 20,000 kilometers (12,400 miles), with a normal cruising altitude between 18 and 20 kilometers (59,000 and 66,000 feet) and a cruising speed of roughly Mach 0.5 to 0.65. Some sources have suggested the aircraft was developed by Nantong University in Jiangsu province, though this has not been independently confirmed.
Satellite imagery from Malan has also shown a second large flying-wing aircraft nearby, described by analysts as a heavier “cranked-kite” design with a wingspan of roughly 42 meters (137 feet), likely intended for lower-altitude missions and potentially capable of both surveillance and long-range strike. The War Zone has also identified a smaller, tailless drone resembling China’s sixth-generation fighter designs parked at the same base, alongside a Y-20 heavy transport aircraft, suggesting Malan supports multiple secretive aircraft programs simultaneously rather than a single project.
Analysts caution that appearing in satellite photos does not mean the WZ-X is an operational weapon. Its exact role, whether reconnaissance, communications relay or long-range strike, along with its manufacturer and formal designation, remains unconfirmed.

articles.title: Trump sends Witkoff, Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv with new Ukraine peace plan
articles.body:
Trump sends Witkoff, Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv with new Ukraine peace plan
The US envoys are carrying a proposal to end the war in Ukraine and are due to meet Putin and Zelensky as drone strikes escalate
US President Donald Trump said on Friday he was sending envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv with a plan to end more than four years of war in Ukraine.
The move marks Washington’s latest bid to break a diplomatic stalemate in Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II, which began with Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
A senior Ukrainian official said the envoys were due in Kyiv on Sunday.
US outlet Axios reported they would meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday, and then Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky in Kyiv on Sunday. The Kremlin declined to comment.
Trump told reporters that the two negotiators would seek to gauge whether progress towards peace was possible.
Peace efforts have stalled due to Washington’s war with Iran, while Moscow and Kyiv have intensified long-range attacks, driving up civilian casualties to levels not seen since the start of fighting.

articles.title: US peace envoys Witkoff and Kushner to visit Kyiv and Moscow with plan to 'end war'
articles.body:
The announcement came as Russian strikes on Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region killed four overnight, per local authorities.
US peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are believed to have arrived in Russia ahead of meetings with officials from Moscow and Kyiv this weekend.
The pair come armed with a "proposal to end the war," US President Donald Trump has announced, as the US makes its latest push to break a diplomatic deadlock over the war in Ukraine.
"I sent Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, two great negotiators. They've done a great job, and we sent them over to see whether or not we can get something done. And there may be a good chance that we'll do it," Trump told reporters on Friday.
The duo is then due to head to Kyiv on Sunday, in what will be their first visits to the Ukrainian capital since Trump returned to the White house in January last year.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the planned visit to Ukraine in a post on X.
"We need to look for real options for how to move this war toward an end," Zelenskyy wrote. "We will see what proposals Steve and Jared bring and what they are told in Moscow in response".
He added that Ukrainian forces would ensure the "normal functioning of Russian airspace" to ensure the envoys could make the trip to Moscow safely.
Zelenskyy had warned airlines and insurers on Tuesday that Russian airspace would "effectively be closing" due to the scale of Ukrainian drone operations making flying unsafe.
But the Ukrainian leader said Ukraine would hold off on strikes while Witkoff and Kushner made the trip, while calling on Moscow to do the same.
"We are looking out for them, not for Russia. There will be no air strikes from our side, and Russia must do the same, ensuring there are no air strikes from its side for the time needed to hold these talks and handle the logistical matters related to this American visit," he wrote on social media.
Russian strikes kill four overnight
The announcement came as Russian strikes on the city of Kamianske in Ukraine's Dnipropetrovsk region killed four overnight, per local authorities.
Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration, said five people were also injured in the strikes, which hit an industrial facility.
On Friday, Zelenskyy announced that a Russian drone had also hit the headquarters of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) in central Kyiv, adding that it had been "aimed directly" at the head of the agency's office.
In response to the attack, he said he had ordered the SBU to carry out an "appropriate, tangible response and, where possible, one that mirrors this strike."
Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia had also struck airports in Kyiv and Boryspil overnight, calling them "deliberate" and a "reaction" to the planned envoy meetings.
"We have taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace," he wrote on X.

articles.title: Majority of Poles believe Russian provocations against Poland are likely
articles.body:
Majority of Poles believe Russian provocations against Poland are likely
Almost two-thirds of Poles (64.9%) believe that warnings about further Russian provocations against Poland are credible.
Source: the results of a SW Research poll commissioned by Onet, as reported by European Pravda
Details: When asked, "Do you consider warnings about possible new Russian provocations against Poland credible?", 64.9% of respondents answered in the affirmative. Some 29.4% answered "definitely yes", while 37.2% said "probably yes".
A total of 18.8% of respondents expressed the opposite view. The option "definitely no" was chosen by 7.6%, while 11.6% answered "probably no". Another 14.3% chose "hard to say".
The SW Research poll commissioned by Onet was conducted from 31 August to 1 September 2026 using computer-assisted web interviewing (CAWI). As part of the study, 800 interviews were conducted among a nationwide sample of adults. A quota sample was used to ensure representativeness by gender, age and the population size of the respondents' cities.
Background:
- This week, Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said that his country is strengthening the protection of its airspace due to recent provocations by Russia.
- From 10 September to 9 December 2026, eastern Poland will be included in the EP R134 temporary restricted airspace zone.
- On 30 July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile manufactured in the second quarter of 2026 at a plant in the Moscow Oblast fell in Lublin Voivodeship.
- Earlier, media reported that Poland, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia are cooperating on protecting against potential Russian attacks on infrastructure in these countries, which could be carried out under a "false flag", as allied intelligence agencies have repeatedly warned.

articles.title: Sanctions or illusion? US claim on Iran’s financial lifeline
articles.body:
In his latest remarks, the US Treasury Secretary has once again presented an exaggerated picture of Washington’s ability to collapse Iran’s economic network, claiming that by sanctioning a Turkish bank, the United States has cut “Iran’s vital financial arteries”—a claim that, rather than reflecting a decisive development in Iran’s economy, reflects the Donald Trump administration’s effort to instill the impression that sanctions are on the verge of completely paralyzing Iran’s economy.
Scott Bessent, the US Treasury Secretary, announced on Friday that Washington has sanctioned the investment bank “Golden Global” and two of its subsidiaries in Turkey. The US Treasury Department claims that this group has played a role in transferring Iran’s oil revenues from China to Turkey and converting part of these resources into cash and gold, and has also provided banking services to some Iranian entities. At the same time, Bessent warned that another bank may be targeted by sanctions next week and even spoke of continuing this process until other countries stop economic cooperation with Iran.
The sanction itself is, of course, a reality and cannot be denied. The United States has placed a financial institution based in Turkey on its sanctions list, and this action severely restricts its access to the dollar-based financial system. But there is a very large gap between “sanctioning a bank” and “cutting a country’s financial arteries.” That gap is precisely where the Trump administration’s propaganda rhetoric enters the scene.
Iran has been under the harshest US sanctions regime for years and has redesigned an important part of its financial and trade network to cope with these very pressures. Tehran is not dependent on a single bank, a single money transfer route, or a single country to continue its foreign trade. Exchange networks, indirect trade, barter, the use of non-dollar currencies, intermediary companies, and cooperation with various trading partners are part of the mechanisms that have been developed over recent years to reduce the impact of sanctions. Therefore, even if one channel is closed, it does not mean that all of Iran’s financial flows have stopped.
More importantly, the very sanctioning of Golden Global shows that Washington is still identifying and targeting Iran’s financial “channels”; that is, if all of Iran’s financial arteries had truly already been cut, there would have been no need to discover and sanction new routes. The fact that the US Treasury Department goes after new banks, companies, and intermediaries every week actually shows that Iran’s trade and resource-transfer network remains active, and Washington is trying to restrict it step by step.
On the other hand, another part of Bessent’s remarks about oil prices is also significantly out of step with market reality. He predicted that an increase in global supply could bring crude oil prices down to the range of $40 to $50. But with military and geopolitical tensions in the Middle East continuing, the oil market is not currently confirming such a picture. Brent crude traded at around $95 in Friday’s trading and rose more than 6 percent over the course of a week. More simply, the current market is not only not in the $40 to $50 range, but is almost double the level the US Treasury Secretary is talking about.
This gap between claim and reality is highly significant. The Trump administration is trying to convey two messages at the same time: first, that US economic pressure against Iran is choking the country’s economy; and second, that Washington is capable of sharply lowering oil prices by increasing energy supply. But the oil market is not subject to the decisions of a single government. War, geopolitical risk, shipping routes, the security of the Strait of Hormuz, the export volumes of major producers, and market expectations all play a role in determining oil prices.
Even from a political perspective, the claim of “cutting Iran’s financial arteries” is more of a threatening message to foreign banks and companies than a report on the collapse of Iran’s economy. The United States wants to convince banks and financial institutions in Turkey, the UAE, China, and other countries that cooperating with Iran will come at a heavy cost. In fact, the main goal of secondary sanctions is precisely this: Washington wants to extend the power of its sanctions beyond US borders and force companies in other countries to choose between trading with Iran and access to the US financial system. This policy undoubtedly creates costs for Iran, and the effects of financial and banking sanctions cannot be minimized. The narrowing of money transfer routes, the increase in the cost of foreign trade, the greater difficulty of repatriating export revenues, and the increased risk for banks and companies doing business all create real pressure. But economic pressure is not the same as economic collapse, and sanctioning one bank is not equivalent to destroying a country’s financial network.
Even inside Iran, economic officials have emphasized in recent days that the country’s economy, despite the pressure of sanctions and restrictions caused by the war, still has resources and tools for managing the foreign exchange market. The governor of the Central Bank of Iran has also announced that the country has sufficient foreign exchange resources and that the central bank is ready to intervene to manage the market. Of course, these statements do not mean there are no economic problems; rather, they show that the image of a “collapsed economy” raised in Washington’s rhetoric is far from the complex reality of Iran’s economy.
Ultimately, what Bessent calls an “economic isolation operation” should be seen more as a maximum-pressure campaign and a continuous economic war against Iran, rather than a final blow intended to disable the country’s economy. The United States can raise the cost of trading with Iran, sanction banks, and target financial routes one after another; but to conclude from these measures that “Iran’s financial arteries have been cut” is a claim far larger than the reality that the available evidence shows.
The main problem with such claims is that, through repetition, economic pressure is mistaken for strategic success. Washington may be able to remove a bank from the dollar financial system, but it still has to prove that it can disable all of Iran’s networks of trade, exports, resource transfers, and economic relations with foreign partners. Until that happens, phrases like “cutting Iran’s vital arteries” are more a part of the Trump administration’s psychological operation to display the power of sanctions than an accurate description of Iran’s economic situation.
MNA

articles.title: Putin's envoy Dmitriev to meet Witkoff, Kushner upon their arrival in Moscow, sources say
articles.body:
US envoys Witkoff, Kushner arrive in Moscow for talks on peace in Ukraine, sources say
MOSCOW - US special representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner landed in Moscow on Sept 5 for talks on the war in Ukraine, two people familiar with the visit told Reuters, adding that they were met by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev.
A motorcade, carrying Witkoff, Kushner and Dmitriev, left Moscow’s governmental airport and headed towards the city, a Reuters witness said.
Dmitriev, who told Reuters in June that he had remained in contact with the US negotiators during a pause in their visits to Russia, took part in all their previous meetings with President Vladimir Putin. He also played a role in negotiating US sanction waivers for Russian oil this year.
US President Donald Trump suggested on Sept 4 that the US had a fresh concrete proposal aimed at ending the war, which is now in its fifth year. He did not, however, elaborate on what that proposal would be.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said also on Sept 4 that the two men would fly to Ukraine on Sept 6 after visiting Moscow. In an X post on Sept 5, Zelensky said Russia hit two Ukrainian airports ahead of US envoys’ visit to Kyiv.
A vast gulf remains between Russia and Ukraine on how to end the 4½-year-old war, the deadliest in Europe since World War II.
The Kremlin said on Sept 4 the position that Putin set out in a speech two years ago – that Ukraine should cede the entire territory of four regions claimed by Russia and abandon its plan to join NATO – was “unshakeable”.
Since the last peace talks in February, each side has intensified long-range air attacks deep inside the other’s territory, while the war at sea has also escalated.
On the ground, the front lines have remained largely static, with Russia making only gradual gains in its attempt to take the whole of Ukraine’s Donbas region.
Ukraine’s drone strikes on Russian oil refineries have led to a summer of fuel shortages and rising prices for Russian motorists, while some 30 attacks on giant warehouses belonging mostly to Wildberries, the country's biggest online retailer, have affected the consumer economy.
A Russian drone attack hit the headquarters of Ukraine’s SBU security service in Kyiv on Sept 4 – the 10th consecutive day of heavy attacks on the capital – and Zelensky vowed to retaliate. REUTERS

articles.title: Why the Falklands Is a Pressure Point For the U.K.—and How Milei, Trump Are Stoking Tensions
articles.body:
Argentina’s President Javier Milei has escalated his country’s claim over the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory, warning he will place economic pressure by sanctioning oil companies with operations in the area.
The Falkland Islands are "Argentine, by history and by right, there is no debate about it,” he said in a nationally televised address Thursday evening.
Milei argued the “winds of change blowing around the world” are favorable to Argentina’s long-claimed sovereignty over the South Atlantic archipelago, citing remarks made by his ally, U.S. President Donald Trump, who recently suggested the U.S. would be reviewing its neutrality on the dispute.
The Argentine President flagged a planned oil project in the area as a cause for concern. Within the next 18 months, two companies—one British and the other Israeli—are set to start extractions from the Sea Lion oilfield, which lies north of the islands and holds an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.
Milei described the project as an urgent threat to Argentina’s sovereignty. "If we do not act swiftly, in a few months they will have the material capacity to access the oil that lies underneath our sea—something that has never happened before,” he said.
The Falkland Islands, known in Argentina as “Islas Malvinas,” sit roughly 300 miles from the Argentine coast, and have been a British territory for almost two centuries, but Argentina has never accepted British sovereignty over the area.
Vowing to take action, Milei said he plans to send a bill to Congress to strengthen Argentina’s response to what he views as attacks on its sovereignty.
Responding to the economic threats, the U.K. government reasserted its “unshakeable” commitment to the archipelago on Friday, with British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting insisting: “Milei’s statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands.”
“The U.K. supports the right of the Falkland Islanders to develop their natural resources for their own economic benefit, and this is an integral part of their right to self-determination,” a spokesperson for Prime Minister Andy Burnham told TIME. “We continue to have a diplomatic relationship with Argentina, and from our perspective we want to continue to strengthen that.”
Here’s what to know about the contentious history of the Falkland Islands and why Milei and Trump’s remarks have sparked concern amid mounting geopolitical tensions.
Do the Falklands belong to Britain or Argentina?
The Falklands' defense and foreign policy is handled by the U.K., but otherwise it has an internal government of its own. The territory has its own constitution and as of 1983, residents of the islands have been British citizens.
In a 2013 referendum, Falkland residents voted overwhelmingly in favor of remaining under British rule. The referendum saw 92% of all eligible voters turn out, with 99.8% of votes being “yes.”
“The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British,” Streeting said Friday, pointing to the will of the voters.
The first recorded landing on the island was made in 1690 by English naval captain John Strong. Britain took possession of West Falkland in 1765. France and Spain each had settlements on the islands at different times, but Britain re-established control in 1833 and has since administered the islands.
“Argentina claims the U.K. took the islands as an act of imperialism in the 1830s, but the remedy to colonial acquisition would be self-determination,” says Marc Weller, programme director of the international law programme at U.K.-based think tank Chatham House.
Given the British government’s insistence on Falklanders deciding their future, “it is therefore acting in accordance with the principle of self-determination,” he tells TIME.
Under the rule of military dictator Leopoldo Galtieri, Argentine forces attempted to stake a territorial claim in April 1982, sparking a 74-day war that Britain won.
Argentina has since continued to claim sovereignty over the islands and the rhetoric has become a unifying issue in the country, experts tell TIME.
The issue recently reared its head during Argentina’s victory over England in the semi-finals of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, with some Argentine players holding up a banner reading "Las Malvinas son Argentinas,” which translates to "The Falklands are Argentine.”
“The Argentinian nation is easily united behind this claim through the Falkland Islands. It's a rallying point, and it's perhaps no accident that as the present Argentinean government is in a little bit of trouble, that they have rediscovered the issue,” says Weller, pointing towards Milei’s controversial fiscal policies and falling popularity among the public.
Milei steps up claim over British territory with sanctions threat
Milei has previously ruled out using force to claim the islands, instead pushing for a diplomatic resolution. Still, his newly-announced plans to impose sanctions against oil companies with operations in the area pose an economic threat.
The two petroleum firms heading the Sea Lion oil drilling project have already felt the impact of Milei’s proposed sanctions.
British company Rockhopper Exploration’s stock value fell by around 10% on Friday morning, with Israeli firm Navitas Petroleum stock value falling by at least 4.5%.
“It's an attempt to add some uncertainty, perhaps to inhibit investment,” suggests Weller, adding he’s doubtful any such threats will impact Downing Street’s position on the sovereignty dispute.
Trump says U.S. position on Falklands is under review
The dispute over sovereignty remains a tense geopolitical issue. China, for example, has been vocal in its support of Argentina’s claim, encouraging negotiations to take place on the matter.
The U.S., meanwhile, has historically recognized the U.K.’s “administration of the islands,” but has maintained a neutral position regarding sovereignty.
However, Trump has indicated that the U.S. may be open to reversing that position.
The Falklands sovereignty became a talking point in April as the U.S. and Europe drifted on account of Trump lambasting European leaders for refusing to get actively involved in the Iran war.
A leaked Pentagon email, which reportedly suggested various ways the Administration could punish NATO allies it believes let the U.S. down, suggested a review of the U.S. position on Britain’s claim to the Falkland Islands, according to Reuters.
Earlier this week, when asked if the U.S. position on the islands was under review, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office: “I always review every position. That's just one of many."
In an interview with a British broadcast channel that aired on Thursday, Trump did not directly respond when asked if the U.S. would come to the U.K’s aid if Argentina claimed the Falklands.
Trump instead pivoted to discuss the Iran war, repeating his claims that the U.K. let him down. “Your country was not there to help me,” he insisted.
When approached by TIME, a spokesperson for Burnham said such comments “are a matter for the U.S. President.”
TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Andrew Gawthorpe, a lecturer at Leiden University and an expert in the foreign policy of the U.S., tells TIME a Washington reversal on the issue “would be an enormous defeat for the U.K. diplomatically and a huge blow” to the special U.K.-U.S. relationship.
Weller agrees, adding that if any U.S. policy were to go against the territorial integrity of the U.K., then “Britain would have to respond quite strongly.”
Trump’s remarks on the Falklands this week could prove difficult for Burnham, who inherited a splintered Washington-London relationship upon replacing Keir Starmer as Prime Minister in July.
“On the one hand, Burnham needs to appear like a strong leader,” says Gawthorpe. “But on the other hand, I think he's very aware that he needs to not annoy Trump any more than is strictly necessary.”

articles.title: Ukraine war: how escalating attacks are upending lives in Kyiv
articles.body:
Ukraine war: how escalating attacks are upending lives in Kyiv
Russia is now using more jet-powered drones, which are faster and harder for Ukraine to intercept than propeller-powered models
Commuters stranded; children rushed underground in the middle of the school day; festivals cancelled; walks punctuated by booming air defences. Near-constant drone attacks are the stark new reality in Kyiv, and daily life is likely to get harder.
Kyiv has survived many traumas since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Despite the initial shock of war and the advent of attack drones and ballistic missiles, residents adapted and managed to impose a semblance of normality.
But as a fifth full winter of war approaches, that is becoming harder to maintain.
Over the summer, Moscow began sending swarms of high-speed, jet-propelled drones that are more destructive and harder to shoot down than older propeller-powered models.
For the last 10 days, air attacks have been around-the-clock rather than mainly at night, puncturing Ukrainians’ sense that their country’s own long-range drone campaign against Russia was swinging the war back in their favour.
